Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents

Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive
Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents

Flex-RSI Team
Abstract

Frontier language models are increasingly deployed as agents, and how well an agent performs depends not only on its model but also on its harness: the prompts, tools, memory, and control loop through which the model acts. When an agent is applied to a new problem, a natural question is whether it can use the feedback of the task to improve the way it works, and not merely its answer. Most existing benchmarks keep the agent’s harness fixed and score the solution it produces, or target large-scale model training. We introduce Flex-RSI, a benchmark for the recursive self-improvement of agents on vision and robotics tasks under a fixed budget. In each round, an executor improves the task solution, which is kept only if it scores higher on held-out validation data, and an improver then revises the harness, including the executor and itself. Every run starts from the same general-purpose harness, and the final solution is scored on hidden test data. Evaluating closed-source and open-weight models on tasks spanning perception, reasoning, robot action, 3D reconstruction, visual creation, and infrastructure, we find that self-improvement helps most when the agent builds its own solution, that feedback recording only success or failure holds back open-weight models, and that open-weight models fall furthest behind where outputs must pass strict checks of physical stability or exact correctness. Paired runs further show that editing the harness itself contributes to the gains.

1  Introduction

Frontier large language models now routinely act as agents that write code, conduct experiments, and read the results over multiple steps (Anthropic, 2026a; OpenAI, 2026b; Google DeepMind, 2026; Qwen Team, 2026b; DeepSeek-AI, 2026; GLM-5 Team, 2026). An agent’s performance depends not only on the underlying model but also on its harness: the prompts, tools, memory, and control loop through which the model acts. This raises a practical question for anyone who deploys an agent on a new problem: given only the task, can the agent use the task’s feedback to improve the way it works under a fixed budget, and not merely its answer?

Most existing benchmarks run each model inside a fixed harness, often the vendor’s own, and score only the solution or artifact it produces, mostly on machine-learning research tasks with a continuous metric (Chan et al., 2025; Wijk et al., 2024); those that also let the agent revise its harness (RSI-Exam Team, 2026) or that center on upstream model training at scale (OpenRSI Foundation, 2026) remain within machine-learning research. We introduce Flex-RSI to measure how well a frontier agent improves both its solution and its own harness on general vision and robotics tasks, a setting in which agents are increasingly deployed, each attempt consumes real compute, and the goal is a better solution within hours to days.

In Flex-RSI, the harness consists of two components that alternate over rounds (Figure 1a). The executor improves the task solution: it modifies the solution, runs experiments, and evaluates them on the labeled development data, and its candidate is kept only if it also scores higher on held-out validation data. The improver then reviews the round and modifies the harness itself, including the executor’s prompts, tools, and workflow as well as its own prompts, settings, and lessons. Every run starts from the same general-purpose harness and, on each task, the same starter solution.

The tasks differ in what the agent must produce (a single answer or a solution it builds), how the evaluator scores it (on a scale or only as success or failure), and how strictly the output is checked. From experiments on 24 tasks spanning perception, reasoning, robot action, 3D reconstruction, visual creation, and infrastructure (Figure 1b), with 18 closed-source and open-weight models, we find:

  1. 1.

    Tasks in which the agent builds the solution leave more room for self-improvement: tasks whose solution is a single answer to each question leave little room to improve, while tasks in which the agent builds its own solution leave the most, and there models pull apart (Figure 1c).

  2. 2.

    The granularity of feedback matters: feedback that scores each episode on a scale helps all models, whereas feedback that records only success or failure leaves open-weight models barely improving on the solutions they build.

  3. 3.

    Strict checks of physical stability and exact correctness pose the greatest challenge: outputs that look plausible often fail checks of physical stability or exact correctness, and open-weight models fall furthest behind on them.

Paired runs further show that letting the improver edit the harness raises the test score in six of seven pairs of otherwise identical runs (Section 5.4).

2  Related work

2.1  Benchmarks for self-improving agents

Benchmarks for machine-learning engineering and scientific research measure whether agents can turn a task description into a working result. MLE-bench evaluates machine-learning engineering on competition tasks (Chan et al., 2025); RE-Bench compares agents with human experts on research-engineering problems (Wijk et al., 2024); and PaperBench assesses the replication of machine-learning research (Starace et al., 2025). Related evaluations examine the design and execution of machine-learning experiments (Huang et al., 2023b) and the generation of executable programs for data-driven scientific discovery (Chen et al., 2025). Their primary evaluation targets are the models, code, and research results that an agent produces.

Evaluations framed around recursive self-improvement cover several different objects of improvement. RSI-Exam supports executable research on both task methods and harnesses for frozen models, followed by hidden-test evaluation (RSI-Exam Team, 2026). OpenRSI Index spans foundation-model development, including large-scale training and lighter-weight inference, agent, and systems tasks (OpenRSI Foundation, 2026). Autonomous post-training is evaluated through controlled training runs and assessments of the resulting models (Rank et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026c), while algorithm-design tasks ask agents to improve training procedures that are subsequently evaluated by retraining (Chi et al., 2026). Sustained machine-learning research with repeated validation feedback and a separate hidden test is evaluated in AutoResearchExam (Ramesh et al., 2026). Harness engineering also appears alongside model-training tasks in Vals RSI Index (Chen et al., 2026b). TraceTrial-Bench evaluates the reliability of agent harnesses themselves rather than their improvement (Cao et al., 2026). These settings share an interest in autonomous experimentation, but differ in whether the optimized artifact is data, a training algorithm, model weights, or the harness around a model.

Complementary studies examine how experience becomes reusable improvement. Data-centric research under a fixed post-training stack is studied in RSIBench-Data (Meng et al., 2026). Procedural-ability transfer and the conversion of episodic experience into reusable skills are evaluated in EvoAgentBench (Gao et al., 2026b) and SkillEvolBench (Lei et al., 2026), respectively. EvolveTool-Bench checks whether evolved tools satisfy independent conformance tests beyond completing the current task (Kaliyev and Maryanskyy, 2026). The contribution of persistent experience to later personal-agent behavior is isolated through matched persistence-on/off comparisons in PAST-Bench (Xue et al., 2026). Whether self-evolving language-model agents learn new tasks without forgetting earlier ones is evaluated in a related study (Chen et al., 2026e). EmbodiedCLBench evaluates whether embodied agents can reuse the experience gained on basic tasks to solve unseen compositions of them (Huang et al., 2026b), and Embodied Skill Bench measures how packaged embodied skills help agents on physical tasks (Han et al., 2026c). Together, these studies motivate evaluating both immediate task gains and improvements that remain useful on subsequent tasks.

Flex-RSI studies task-solution and harness improvement together on vision, robotics, and related downstream tasks. For each task, every model starts from the same general-purpose harness and starter solution, then alternates execution and harness revision under a fixed budget. The improver can edit the executor’s prompts, tools, and workflow as well as its own prompts, settings, and lessons. This shared protocol separates three questions: how much the task solution improves, what additional gains come from editing the harness, and whether a harness built by one model helps another model on the same task. A review of the evidence behind recursive self-improvement claims finds that few studies compare improvement procedures from identical starting artifacts at a matched budget (Chen et al., 2026g); the paired runs with and without the improver (Section 5.4) make this comparison.

2.2  Frontier agents

Language-model agents connect reasoning to actions and environmental feedback through an execution loop. ReAct interleaves reasoning and tool use (Yao et al., 2023), Reflexion carries verbal feedback into subsequent trials through episodic memory (Shinn et al., 2023), and Voyager accumulates executable skills through open-ended interaction in Minecraft (Wang et al., 2023). Coding interfaces such as Claude Code and Codex CLI expose file editing and command execution (Anthropic, 2026c; OpenAI, 2026d). OpenHands provides infrastructure for software-development agents (Wang et al., 2025b), while SWE-agent studies how an agent–computer interface supports repository navigation, editing, and testing (Yang et al., 2024). Research agents extend these capabilities to experimentation: AIDE searches over candidate solution code (Jiang et al., 2025), and The AI Scientist combines research ideation, experiments, paper writing, and review in an automated workflow (Lu et al., 2024). Frontier models have also been evaluated as robot agents that act in the control loop (Huang et al., 2026a; Zhou et al., 2026b; Yao et al., 2026c) or write reusable robot tools (Ge et al., 2026), across many embodiments (Yang et al., 2026b) and against learned policies (Zhang et al., 2026f), and coding agents have been asked to reconstruct dynamic scenes as executable graphics programs (Shen et al., 2026a).

Automated agent design makes parts of this execution machinery optimization variables. Promptbreeder evolves both task prompts and the mutation prompts that revise them (Fernando et al., 2023), while GEPA uses reflection on execution traces to propose and select prompt updates (Agrawal et al., 2026). ADAS searches over agent programs using an archive of prior designs (Hu et al., 2025), and AFlow searches over code-represented workflows (Zhang et al., 2025b). A builder model can also learn principles for constructing the execution environment of a fixed target model (Qian et al., 2026). AlphaEvolve applies evolutionary program search to scientific and algorithmic discovery, with executable evaluators selecting candidate task programs (Novikov et al., 2025). These approaches optimize objects ranging from prompts to complete programs, with different boundaries around the optimization procedure itself.

Self-modifying agents extend this search to their own implementations. STOP applies its code improver to the improver itself (Zelikman et al., 2024); Gödel Agent and SICA likewise revise agent logic and orchestration code (Yin et al., 2025; Robeyns et al., 2025). The Darwin Gödel Machine retains an archive of empirically evaluated, self-modified agents (Zhang et al., 2025a), while the Huxley–Gödel Machine also considers a candidate’s potential to produce better descendants (Wang et al., 2026d). Meta-Harness searches harness code using previous candidates, scores, and execution traces (Lee et al., 2026b). RHI represents the harness as a prompt-level specification of the agent loop and refines it using pairwise feedback over its own revision history (Lee et al., 2026a). Self-Harness uses execution failures to guide revisions to the model’s own harness (Zhang et al., 2026a), and AIDE2 recursively revises research-agent code (Srikanth et al., 2026).

Several systems explicitly distinguish task improvement from improvement of the process that produces it. Hyperagents combine a task agent and a meta agent in a shared editable program, allowing the self-modification mechanism itself to evolve and studying transfer of meta-level improvements (Zhang et al., 2026b). HSI separates a task harness, an evolver, and a meta-evolver under a fixed outer anchor (Zhou, 2026). In robotics, RegenHarness revises harness configuration from execution records, with regression checks and release gates governing acceptance (Wang et al., 2026a). Harness evolution around frozen models now spans video understanding (Luo et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026), image generation with a frozen generator (Han et al., 2026a), 3D reconstruction (Yao et al., 2026a), and embodied agents, including robot manipulation, where the harness is revised from diagnosed execution failures (Tian et al., 2026a; Feng et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026b; Du et al., 2026), experience is organized into knowledge or executable stacks shared across tasks (Bao et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026f; Wen et al., 2026), the system decides where to spend robot trials (Song et al., 2026), and changes are tested in simulation before they reach the robot (Hu et al., 2026). Studies of these loops find that the number of rollouts the optimizer sees in each round and the selection rule determine whether an evolved robot harness generalizes (Wei et al., 2026b), that accepting any edit that raises an aggregate validation score admits regressions and favors noise (Wang et al., 2026e), that proxy improvements need not hold where the update is deployed (Wang et al., 2026b), and that an exact validation score after every attempt opens the validation split to adaptive selection (Yao et al., 2026b). RRSI addresses the risk that harness evolution overfits its training tasks, with gains that shrink or vanish on out-of-distribution benchmarks, by constraining how edits are proposed and selected (Xia et al., 2026). Other studies ask which failures harness evolution can repair and when weight training should take over (Tian et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026c), argue that rewriting the scaffold around frozen weights avoids diminishing returns but not an eventual ceiling (Bobadilla-Suarez et al., 2026), and report that weak evaluators and early failures in long skill chains stall improvement over long robot runs (Wang, 2026). Surveys organize these developments by the components that evolve and the feedback that drives their updates (Gao et al., 2026a; Fang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026a), and recent surveys and position papers cover recursive self-improvement in physical AI (Han et al., 2026b; Zhou et al., 2026a), agent harnesses for video generation (Fan et al., 2026), and the use of frontier models for 3D modeling, computational design, and robotics (Dou et al., 2026).

These systems propose particular ways to accumulate experience, search for agent designs, or revise an improvement procedure. Flex-RSI evaluates the ability to make such revisions through a shared executor–improver harness (Section 3.2). Each frontier model operates both components from the same initial harness and, on each task, the same starter solution and budget. The executor changes the task solution; the improver changes the executor and its own instructions and lessons. The evaluator, data splits, and budget accounting remain fixed. This setting makes the model’s capacity to improve its operating machinery the object of comparison across vision, robotics, and related tasks, while keeping changes to the solution distinct from changes to the harness.

2.3  Flex-RSI tasks

Flex-RSI draws its 24 tasks from six areas, combining established benchmarks, source datasets, and our own curated creation tasks. Table 1 summarizes their sources and metrics. Each task provides a starter solution, development data, hidden validation and test splits, and a fixed improvement budget, so that these resources support the evaluation of changes to both task solutions and agent harnesses.

Action

The manipulation tasks use simulated environments from RoboDojo (Chen et al., 2026d) and RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026), which extends RoboCasa’s household simulation platform (Nasiriany et al., 2024). Active Search uses H*Bench’s panoramic environments for visual search (Yu et al., 2026a), while RoboLab uses the RoboLab-120 suite to evaluate a generalist tabletop manipulation policy (Yang et al., 2026a). The LIBERO-based tasks (Liu et al., 2023) examine robustness to changes in initial conditions and task specifications through LIBERO-PRO (Zhou et al., 2025), and adaptation to changes during execution through LIBERO-MAX (Zhang et al., 2026e). Embodied-SWE draws on EmbodiedSWE-Bench, where agents write robot-control programs and receive scores based on physical task progress (Shen et al., 2026b). Related simulation benchmarks extend such evaluation to whole-body humanoid loco-manipulation, as in SIMPLE (Wei et al., 2026a).

Reasoning

Ego-Exo Memory uses the Ego-Exo4D portion of EgoExoMem for memory reasoning across synchronized first- and third-person videos (Liu et al., 2026b; Grauman et al., 2024). Kinematics uses QuantiPhy to infer physical quantities such as sizes, velocities, and accelerations from video (Puyin et al., 2026); Mass adapts product photographs and metadata from Amazon Berkeley Objects for weight estimation (Collins et al., 2022). Abstract reasoning spans grid transformations in ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2 (Chollet, 2019; Chollet et al., 2025) and interactive exploration in ARC-AGI-3 (ARC Prize Foundation, 2026). Spatial-VSI uses VSI-Bench’s spatial questions about indoor videos (Yang et al., 2025).

Creation

Image Editing uses our own curated images and editing instructions, and Text-to-Image uses original Chinese and English prompts. Multi-turn Editing follows the five-turn sessions of MSE-Bench, introduced with VINCIE, in which each instruction acts on the previous result (Qu et al., 2026). Video Generation uses the compositional prompts and evaluation criteria of T2V-CompBench (Sun et al., 2025).

Reconstruction

3D Tracking adapts IGGT’s instance-tracking setting (Li et al., 2026) on ScanNet and ScanNet++ (Dai et al., 2017; Yeshwanth et al., 2023). Scene from Photo uses HARMONY300, introduced with HARMONY for reconstructing furnished rooms from single images (Sun et al., 2026); its synthetic scenes derive from 3D-FRONT (Fu et al., 2021). Scene from Video uses the indoor scenes released with HoloScene (Xia et al., 2025), drawn from Replica and ScanNet++ (Straub et al., 2019; Yeshwanth et al., 2023), together with CoDimRecon’s geometry, rendering, and physical-stability evaluation setting (Xie et al., 2026).

Perception

Visual Search combines high-resolution questions from V*Bench and HR-Bench 8K (Wu and Xie, 2024; Wang et al., 2025a). Video Quality combines subjective quality scores for YouTube-UGC videos (Wang et al., 2019; Yim et al., 2020) with human preferences on generated-video pairs from Rapidata’s Veo 3.1 comparison dataset (Rapidata, 2025).

Infrastructure

VAE Decode uses the variational autoencoder released with MiniMax H3 (MiniMax, 2026b) and asks the agent to accelerate its decoder while preserving the reference outputs on unseen inputs.

3  Flex-RSI

Flex-RSI evaluates whether an agent, given a task and a fixed budget, can improve not only its solution to the task but also the harness through which it operates. We first define the task setting (Section 3.1), then the self-improving harness (Section 3.2), and finally how runs are evaluated (Section 3.3).

3.1  Problem setup

Each task provides the agent with a starter solution, compute resources, a budget, and data partitioned into three disjoint splits. The development split, including its labels, is available to the agent for experimentation and evaluation. The validation split is withheld from the agent and determines which candidate solutions are retained. The test split is likewise withheld and is used only once, after the run terminates, to evaluate the final solution. The objective of the agent is to maximize the test score of its final solution within the budget.

On a given task, every run starts from the same starter solution and is subject to the same budget, which limits wall-clock time, GPU hours, model usage, the number of validation evaluations, and the number of rounds. The 24 tasks are listed in Table 1 and described in Appendix A.

3.2  The self-improving harness

A harness is the program that mediates between a language model and a task. Through its prompts, tools, control loop, and memory, it determines the context presented to the model and the actions available to it. Since the harness consists of code and text, the agent can modify it in the same manner as any other program, while the model weights remain fixed. In Flex-RSI, the harness H=(E,I)H=(E,I) comprises two components that query the same model. The executor EE operates on the task solution: it modifies the solution, conducts experiments, and evaluates the results on the development split. The improver II operates on the harness: it analyses the executor’s trajectories and results, diagnoses failures, and revises the prompts, tools, and workflow of the executor as well as its own instructions and accumulated lessons.

Let s0s_{0} denote the starter solution, 𝒟dev\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{dev}}, 𝒟val\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}}, and 𝒟test\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}} the development, validation, and test splits, and S⁡(s,𝒟)S(s;\mathcal{D}) the score that the task evaluator assigns to a solution ss on a split 𝒟\mathcal{D}. A run starts from the harness H0=(E0,I0)H_{0}=(E_{0},I_{0}) and proceeds over rounds t=1,2,…t=1,2,\dots. In round tt, the executor of the current harness modifies the accepted solution st−1s_{t-1}, using only the development split, and submits a candidate

s~t=Et−1​(st−1,𝒟dev).\tilde{s}_{t}=E_{t-1}\bigl(s_{t-1};\,\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{dev}}\bigr). (1)

The candidate is then evaluated on the validation split and retained only if it improves on the accepted solution by more than a noise margin δ\delta, which the starting harness sets to twice the standard deviation of the starter’s validation score and which the improver may revise (Appendix B):

st={s~tif ​S​(s~t,𝒟val)>S⁡(st−1,𝒟val)+δ,st−1otherwise.s_{t}=\begin{cases}\tilde{s}_{t}&\text{if }S(\tilde{s}_{t};\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}})>S(s_{t-1};\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{val}})+\delta,\\ s_{t-1}&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (2)

Finally, the improver examines the records τ1:t\tau_{1:t} of all rounds so far, which comprise the executor’s trajectories, experiments, and scores, and produces the harness for the next round:

(Et,It)=It−1(Et−1,It−1;τ1:t).(E_{t},\,I_{t})=I_{t-1}\bigl(E_{t-1},\,I_{t-1};\,\tau_{1:t}\bigr). (3)

The run terminates at the round TT in which the budget is exhausted or progress stops (Appendix B), and its result is the final solution sTs_{T}.

Equation 3 makes the recursion explicit: the improver is both the operator that produces the next harness and one of its arguments, so that a modification of II changes how all subsequent modifications are made. The decomposition also separates the two kinds of improvement. A change to the solution takes effect only after it has been confirmed on data unseen by the agent (Equation 2), whereas a change to the harness is reflected in the candidates of subsequent rounds (Equation 1).

All runs start from the same general-purpose harness H0H_{0}, which contains no task- or model-specific components. The evaluator SS, the data splits, and the accounting of the budget are fixed and cannot be modified by the agent. Differences between runs can therefore be attributed to the agents themselves, and runs of different models on the same task are directly comparable.

3.3  Evaluation

We report the test score of the final solution, S⁡(sT,𝒟test)S(s_{T};\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}), and its improvement over the starter solution, S⁡(sT,𝒟test)−S⁡(s0,𝒟test)S(s_{T};\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}})-S(s_{0};\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{test}}). Agent code is executed in a sandbox without access to the validation or test data, so no run can read the held-out data.

4  Experiments

This section reports what the agents achieve, in the order in which a reader would ask about it: how well each model does over all tasks and within each area (Section 4.2), how much of that is due to self-improvement (Section 4.3), in which rounds the gains arrive (Section 4.4), and what they cost (Section 4.5). It reports what happens; Section 5 examines why.

4.1  Models and setup

We evaluate 18 models, comprising 11 closed-source models, namely Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic, 2026a), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Anthropic, 2026b), GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026b), GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI, 2026c), GPT-5.6 Sol (OpenAI, 2026a), Gemini 4 Argon (Google, 2026b), Gemini 3.8 Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026), Gemini 3.7 Flash (Google, 2026a), Grok 4.6 (xAI, 2026), Muse Spark 1.3 (Meta, 2026a), and Muse Wonder 1.0 (Meta, 2026b), and 7 open-weight models, namely Qwen3.8-27B and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (Qwen Team, 2026b), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026a), Gemma-4-31B-it (Gemma Team, 2026), MiniMax-M3 (MiniMax, 2026a), GLM-5.3 Flash (GLM-5 Team, 2026), and DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026).11 1 We evaluate the 1017 version of DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash; it is referred to as DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash throughout. Closed-source models are accessed through their providers’ interfaces, and open-weight models are served on our own GPUs. Every model operates within the same starting harness (Section 3.2) and, on a given task, under the same budget.

How results are reported

Each model is run once on each task it is evaluated on; where a run was repeated, the latest run is reported. RoboDojo and RoboCasa are suites of 10 and 8 robot tasks, each run separately for 10 rounds and aggregated into one suite score. A run’s result is the test score of its final solution on the task’s primary metric, on a 0–100 scale. Because the metrics differ across tasks, models are compared through ranks: on each task, a model scores the share of the other models evaluated on the task that it beats, from 0 (last) to 100 (first). Its score in an area is the mean over the tasks of the area it was run on, and its overall score is the mean of its five area scores. To measure self-improvement itself, we also report the validation score of the starter solution and the best validation score reached during the run. The main results cover the 20 tasks evaluated with at least six models; the four tasks evaluated with two models so far are reported in Table 12.

4.2  Main results

Figure 2(a) gives one score per model and Figure 2(b) breaks it down by area. Claude Opus 5.5 has the highest score (91.6): it is one of two models run on all 20 tasks and has the best test score on 11 of them. Gemini 4 Argon follows closely (89.0) over the nine tasks it was run on, then GPT-6.1 Sol (77.0) and GPT-6 Astra (65.5). The best open-weight model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (49.1), places fifth, ahead of Gemini 3.8 Flash and Claude Sonnet 5.5. The leaders differ by area: Sol matches Opus and Argon on reasoning but trails them on action and creation, and Astra is weakest on creation. The rest of this section takes the areas in turn; each table gives the test score of every model on every task of the area, and Appendix C adds the starter’s score, the validation scores and the rounds of every run (and the average rank of each model, Table 11).

Action

The model’s solution drives an agent: an active searcher in 360° scenes (Active Search, SPL), one generalist tabletop policy (RoboLab), a Franka arm in two LIBERO variants, a dual-arm ARX X5 robot (RoboDojo, 10 tasks), and a mobile manipulator in a simulated kitchen (RoboCasa, 8 tasks). Opus has the best test score on five of the six tasks, and Argon on Active Search (79.7). The gap between closed-source and open-weight models is widest here: on RoboDojo and RoboCasa the best open-weight models reach 17.8 and 7.5, against 55.1 and 57.5 for Opus. These two suites start from nothing, the starter scoring 0 on validation in 4 of 8 RoboDojo runs and 7 of 10 RoboCasa runs, so a model must first write a working policy before a round can improve the score. Tables 13 and 14 give the results of the two suites task by task.

Reasoning

The model answers memory questions over synchronized egocentric and exocentric video (Ego-Exo Memory), estimates physical quantities from video and images (Kinematics and Mass, mean relative accuracy), and solves ARC-AGI-1 and -2 grid puzzles and the interactive games of ARC-AGI-3. Closed models lead every task: Opus on Ego-Exo Memory (72.5) and Mass (63.5), Sonnet on Kinematics (57.2), Astra on ARC-AGI-1 (99.8), and Sol on ARC-AGI-2 (95.8) and ARC-AGI-3 (44.2). Open-weight models are close on the physical quantities (Qwen3.8-27B scores 62.7 on Mass) but fall away on ARC: the best of them reaches 46.7 on ARC-AGI-2 and 0.9 on ARC-AGI-3. ARC-AGI-3 is also one of the tasks where self-improvement does least, with a median validation score of 3.8 for the starter and 4.1 for the best solution.

Creation

The model edits images from instructions (Image Editing), edits one photo over five turns (Multi-turn Editing), and builds text-to-video workflows around a frozen generator (Video Generation, composition score). Scores are compressed: the 12 models span 60.6 to 74.2 on Image Editing, and the top six on Multi-turn Editing lie within 2.8 points. Open-weight models are most competitive here: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ranks third in the area and scores 91.4 on Video Generation, against 93.9 for Opus.

Reconstruction

The model tracks object instances in 3D (3D Tracking, temporal mIoU) and rebuilds a furnished room from a photo or an indoor scene from a video (scene score). Opus leads all three tasks (79.6, 66.5 and 70.9), 13 to 18 points ahead of the next model, GPT-6 Astra, on the two scene tasks. Reconstruction gains the most from self-improvement: the median validation score rises from 19.4 to 62.2 on 3D Tracking and from 7.7 to 38.0 on Scene from Photo.

Perception

The model finds small targets in high-resolution images (Visual Search, accuracy) and rates the perceptual quality of real user videos (Video Quality). The starters already score high, with a median validation score of 80.0 and 78.2, and the leaders are a few points apart: Gemini 4 Argon scores 98.6 on Visual Search, and on Video Quality GPT-6 Astra (82.1), Claude Opus 5.5 and DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash (82.0) are within 0.1 of each other. With little headroom left, the best open-weight model is 10 points behind on Visual Search and level on Video Quality.

4.3  How much self-improvement adds

The scores above combine what a model can do from the start with what it gains by improving. Figure 3 separates the two by comparing the starter’s validation score with the best validation score reached during the run. Self-improvement raises the validation score in 150 of the 177 runs (85%), by a median of 10.4 points.

The gain depends on how much the task leaves to build. It is largest where the agent builds most of its solution from a weak starter: on 3D Tracking, RoboLab and Active Search the median validation score rises from 19.4, 8.3 and 23.0 to 62.2, 45.8 and 52.7 (Figure 3(a)). It is smallest where the starter already solves most of the task, as on ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2 (median starter 91.9 and 82.5, a median gain of 0 points on both). Two tasks do not fit this pattern: ARC-AGI-3 and Scene from Video start low (3.8 and 17.3) and still barely improve (to 4.1 and 18.5).

The gain also depends on the model. Closed-source models improve more often and by more: they raise the validation score in 94% of their 85 runs, by a median of 14.9 points, against 76% of 92 runs and 8.5 points for open-weight models. Per model (Figure 3(b)), the mean gain ranges from 26.7 points for Claude Opus 5.5 and 25.7 for Gemini 4 Argon to 6.8 for Gemma-4-31B-it, and the four models with the highest scores in Figure 2(a) have four of the five largest gains.

4.4  Improvement over rounds

Figure 4(a) shows in which rounds the gains arrive. For each run that improves, we express its best validation score after every round as a share of the run’s whole gain, and take the median over the runs of each area. Most of the gain comes early: the median run reaches 90% of its gain by round 3 in Perception and Reasoning and by round 4 in Creation. Action and Reconstruction take longer, reaching 90% only by rounds 6 and 8. These are the two areas with the weakest starters (median validation score 16.7 and 19.4, against 60.0 to 78.8 in the other three), where the agent likely has to build a working solution before it can refine it.

4.5  Cost

Runs differ widely in what they spend. A run on one task, counting each robot task of RoboDojo and RoboCasa separately, uses a median of 49.7 million tokens, and the middle 80% of runs use between 8.6 and 93.4 million. We compare tokens rather than prices, since the open-weight models are served on our own GPUs. To compare models on the same footing, Figure 4(b) expresses each model’s token use relative to the median model on the same task. Spending more does not buy a higher score: across the 12 models, the rank correlation between relative token use and score is −0.05-0.05. Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra, three of the four highest-scoring models, use 0.35 to 0.61 times the median, whereas Gemini 4 Argon reaches a score close to that of Opus with 1.66 times. Five of the six open-weight models use at least the median (1.0 to 1.75 times), and all six score below 50.

4.6  Qualitative examples

Figures 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 compare the behavior of solutions before and after self-improvement on robot manipulation, active search, abstract reasoning, image editing, and 3D reconstruction from a photo. Further examples on these and the remaining tasks are given in Appendix D.

5  Analysis and takeaways

Table 7 lists, for every task evaluated with at least six models, the quantities on which the findings of Section 1 rest. The tasks fall into two groups according to what the agent has to produce. On seven tasks, the solution gives a single answer to each question, and the starter solution obtains it by passing the question to a model: the model being evaluated, or on Kinematics and Mass a fixed open-weight model. On the other thirteen, the agent has to build the solution itself, namely a program, a robot policy, or a processing pipeline that produces the output. These thirteen tasks are divided further according to how the task evaluator scores an episode: on nine it assigns a score on a scale, and on four it records only whether the episode or level succeeded. Sections 5.1, 5.2 and 5.3 examine the three findings in turn, and Section 5.4 examines whether editing the harness contributes to the improvement.

5.1  Tasks in which the agent builds the solution leave more room for self-improvement

On tasks whose solution is a single answer, the starter solution already passes each question to the model, so it scores high from the start and its score depends on the model: its median validation score over these seven tasks is 78.2, and the models are 27.5 points apart before the first round (medians over tasks). The largest gain that any run achieves is 14.8 points at the median, and at the end of the runs the models are 25.0 points apart, about as far as at the start. On the tasks in which the agent builds the solution, every model starts from the same program, although its score can depend on the model that it calls. On the nine of them whose evaluator scores each episode on a scale, this program scores 19.4 at the median, the largest gain is 38.8 points at the median, and the models, 0.9 points apart at the start, end 38.8 points apart; on the four whose evaluator records only success or failure, they move from 2.5 to 37.2 points apart. The same pattern appears in Figure 1c. The exceptions are Kinematics, whose solution is a single answer but whose starter solution scores only 27.7 and on which a run gains 33.5 points, and Multi-turn Editing, on which the agent builds the solution but no run gains more than 4.2 points.

5.2  The granularity of feedback matters

On the nine tasks in which the agent builds the solution and the evaluator scores each episode on a scale, the median gain over the open-weight runs of a task is 9.9 points at the median over tasks, against 28.4 for the closed-source runs, and on 3D Tracking and Active Search it is close to that of the closed-source runs (39.8 against 42.8, and 29.3 against 28.4). On the four tasks whose evaluator records only whether an episode or a level succeeded, namely RoboCasa, LIBERO-MAX, LIBERO-PRO, and ARC-AGI-3, the median open-weight gain falls to 1.6 points, while the closed-source runs still gain 16.9. The median open-weight run does not improve at all on LIBERO-PRO and gains 0.2 points on ARC-AGI-3. Since a candidate is retained only if it raises the validation score (Equation 2), a score on a scale rewards a change that improves part of an episode, whereas a score that records only success or failure rewards a change only once it turns failed episodes into successful ones.

5.3  Strict checks of physical stability and exact correctness pose the greatest challenge

The difference between the best closed-source and the best open-weight model is largest on tasks whose evaluator applies such a check: whether a robot task succeeds in simulation (RoboCasa, 50.0 points; RoboLab, 40.3; RoboDojo, 37.3), whether the output grid is exactly right (ARC-AGI-2, 49.2) or a level is cleared (ARC-AGI-3, 43.3; on ARC-AGI-1, whose puzzles the starter solutions already nearly solve, it is 8.8), and whether a reconstructed scene is physically and geometrically consistent (Scene from Video, 36.4; Scene from Photo, 26.5). It is smallest on tasks scored by a judge or with a tolerance: Video Quality (0.1), Mass (0.8), Multi-turn Editing (1.0), Video Generation (2.5), and Image Editing (4.2). The component scores of the two scene tasks show how plausible outputs fail these checks (Tables 29 and 30). On Scene from Photo, the renderings of the open-weight scenes resemble the photo, with an Appearance score of up to 81.8, but the furniture is not recovered as complete and correctly placed objects: their Objects score is at most 16.5, against 62.5 for both closed-source models. On Scene from Video, the Physics score, the fraction of objects that remain stable in simulation, is 0.0 for all four open-weight models, against 70.7 for Claude Opus 5.5 and 37.7 for GPT-6 Astra. The two LIBERO tasks are the exceptions among the robot tasks: the best open-weight model matches the best closed-source model on LIBERO-MAX (45.8) and trails it by 10.0 points on LIBERO-PRO.

5.4  Does editing the harness help?

Table 8 compares pairs of runs that differ only in whether the improver runs. In the run without the improver, labeled frozen harness in the table, the starting harness is never modified; in the run with it, labeled self-improving harness, the improver edits the executor and itself after every round, as in all other runs of this report. The test score with the improver is higher in six of the seven pairs, by 2.0 to 40.0 points; in the seventh, Claude Opus 5.5 on Turn On Sink Faucet reaches 80.0 in both runs, and its run without the improver reached the maximum validation score in round 8. The difference is largest where the unchanged starting harness makes little progress: DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash remains at 0.0 on Open Drawer without the improver and reaches 40.0 with it, and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next gains 20.0 on Turn On Sink Faucet and 38.3 on Active Search. On 3D Tracking, the executor alone already raises the two Qwen models from the 19.4 of the starter solution to validation scores of 48.9 and 63.4, and the improver adds 6.5 and 2.0 points on the test split. The runs without the improver also end after fewer rounds in six of the seven pairs.

Table 9 asks whether a harness built by a stronger model helps a weaker one. On Open Drawer, DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash started from the final executor of Gemini 4 Argon reaches 20.0 when the executor is not modified further and 60.0 when Argon’s final improver continues to edit it, against 40.0 when it improves its own harness from the start and 80.0 for Argon. On Turn On Sink Faucet, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next started from the harness of Claude Opus 5.5 reaches 0.0 in both settings, below the 20.0 it reaches when it improves its own harness and the 80.0 of Opus. On Active Search and 3D Tracking, Qwen3.8-27B started from the final harness of the source run and improved it further with its own improver. On Active Search, it reaches 49.2 from the harness of Gemini 4 Argon, against 69.0 when it improves its own harness from the start and 79.7 for Argon. On 3D Tracking, it reaches 53.8 from the harness of Claude Opus 5.5, against 52.4 from the starting harness and 79.6 for Opus. A harness built by a stronger model thus raised the score of the weaker model on two of the four tasks, by 20.0 points on Open Drawer and 1.4 points on 3D Tracking, and in neither case did the weaker model approach the score of the stronger one.

6  Conclusion

We introduced Flex-RSI, a benchmark that measures whether a frontier agent can improve both its task solution and its own harness within a fixed budget, with every run starting from the same general-purpose harness and every final solution scored on a hidden test split. Across 24 tasks and 18 models, three findings emerge. Self-improvement raises the score most on tasks in which the agent builds its own solution, and on these tasks models that start from the same program end far apart, whereas on tasks whose solution is a single answer the starter solution already scores high and the models end about as far apart as they began. Open-weight models improve when the evaluator scores each episode on a scale, but barely improve when it records only success or failure. The largest gaps between closed-source and open-weight models arise where the evaluator checks physical stability or exact correctness, even when the outputs look plausible. Paired runs further show that editing the harness contributes to the improvement, most where the unchanged starting harness makes little progress, whereas a harness built by a stronger model raised the score of a weaker model on only two of four tasks.

The improvement measured here is mostly at the level of the harness. The evaluated model’s weights never change, and on most tasks no model is trained; on some, the solution may train or fine-tune helper models on the development split. Flex-RSI therefore does not measure a model that modifies its own parameters. Extending the benchmark to weight-level self-improvement, and studying how it interacts with changes to the harness, is left to future work. The leaderboard is maintained on the project page, https://flex-rsi.github.io.
