Appendix A Task cards

This appendix describes each of the 24 tasks of Table 1: what it measures, how its data were built from its source and divided into splits, what the agent has to produce and with which resources, the starter solution, the metric and where it comes from, and the prior work on the source benchmark. Every task follows the setting of Section 3.1: the development split is available to the agent with its labels, while the validation and test splits are withheld. Unless stated otherwise, the solution may call the model being evaluated within the stated limits, and it may not use the annotations of the source benchmark.

A.1  Action

RoboDojo

  • Purpose. Whether the agent can turn a general multimodal model into a closed-loop policy for a dual-arm robot. No policy is trained: the model decides the motions at evaluation time, and the agent improves the program that queries it.

  • Source and construction. Ten simulation tasks of RoboDojo (Chen et al., 2026d). Full credit (success) requires: four bottles in a dustbin, using a handover between the hands; a garment folded with sleeves in and hem aligned to the shoulders; digit tiles placed in the order forming the largest number; three tubes inserted upright into a rack; all five own pieces placed in tic-tac-toe against a randomly playing opponent arm; a T-shaped block pushed onto its pad without lifting; eight xylophone keys struck left to right with a mallet; the conveyor object shown on a board placed in a lifted basket; four eggs in a holder with its lid closed; and five nesting dolls lined up by size. Several tasks also require a return to the start pose. All layouts come from RoboDojo’s evaluation seed 0: per task, validation takes the first five, test the next five, and development the rest, of which a fixed panel of five is evaluated. Validation layouts of three tasks are those of Galbot Team et al. (2026). Tasks with a randomized variant (fold clothes, largest number, Push-T, nesting dolls) use two standard and three randomized layouts per split. The agent sees full development results, the validation score only, and no test results.

  • Setting. An ARX X5 dual-arm robot in Isaac Sim at 25 Hz, run through the pinned single-layout RoboDojo client of RoboICL (Liu et al., 2026a), 500 to 1100 steps per episode, starting in an elbow-up pose slightly in front of RoboDojo’s. The policy receives three RGB cameras, proprioception, and the head-camera calibration, never object poses or rewards, and returns chunks of at most 64 end-effector or joint targets, limited to 3 cm and 0.15 rad per step. It may call the run’s model at most 80 times per episode and no other model; scripted motions and its own inverse kinematics are allowed.

  • Starter solution. One model call per chunk of up to ten end-effector motions, given the head-camera image at 320×240320\times 240, the robot state, and its notes from earlier calls.

  • Metric. Each episode receives the progress score s∈[0,100]s\in[0,100] of its RoboDojo rubric (for example 10, 25, 40, 100 for one to four bottles), as defined in the RoboDojo task documentation (Chen et al., 2026d), 100 only on success, scored as the scene stands when it ends. The task score is St=15​∑est,eS_{t}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{e}s_{t,e} over the test layouts and the suite score 110​∑tSt\frac{1}{10}\sum_{t}S_{t}, a task without a run counting as zero. The success rate is also reported.

  • Prior work. RoboDojo has 42 simulation tasks and evaluates 30 trained manipulation policies (Chen et al., 2026d). Frontier models have also been used as the policy: Galbot Team et al. (2026) reach 48% success on a RoboDojo subset with GPT-6 Astra combined with π0.5\pi_{0.5}; RoboICL (Liu et al., 2026a) conditions the model on demonstrations and interaction memory (overall score 50.64 on 30 tasks against 33.68 for the strongest baseline); and Encore (Kang et al., 2026) writes policy programs from a few demonstrations.

RoboCasa

  • Purpose. Whether the agent can obtain a model-driven policy for a mobile manipulator that carries over from the kitchens and objects used in development to kitchens and objects it has never seen.

  • Source and construction. Eight tasks of RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026), an extension of RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024), with RoboCasa’s own success checks. Six are atomic tasks from RoboCasa365’s seen-task target set: turn on the microwave (on, gripper away from the button), turn on the sink faucet (handle turned over 0.4 rad), open the named cabinet (every door at least 90% open), open the named drawer (at least 95% open), place a mug under the coffee dispenser, and turn off the named burner. Two are composite: portion hot dogs (from its unseen composite set; one bun and one sausage on each of two plates) and kettle boiling (kettle within 15 cm of a burner that is on). An episode is fixed by a kitchen (layout and style), object instances, and a seed from which RoboCasa places the robot and objects and words the instruction. Development has five fixed episodes in RoboCasa’s pretraining kitchens with pretraining objects; validation and test have five episodes each in the same five target kitchens (the first five of RoboCasa’s ten evaluation kitchens) with target objects, differing by seed; validation and test were reduced from ten to five episodes each, and every episode was checked to build and reset. The agent sees full development results, the validation success rate only, and no test results; neither it nor the policy may load target kitchens or objects.

  • Setting. The PandaOmron robot (a Franka Panda arm on a mobile base with a torso lift) in MuJoCo at 20 Hz, with the per-task horizons of RoboCasa’s dataset registry (450 to 2250 steps). The policy receives three 512×512512\times 512 RGB cameras, proprioception, and calibration, never object states, and returns chunks of at most 64 rows of RoboCasa’s 12-dimensional action. It may call the run’s model at most 80 times per episode and no other model.

  • Starter solution. One model call per chunk of up to ten actions, given one base-camera image at 256×256256\times 256, its calibration, the robot state, and its notes from earlier calls.

  • Metric. An episode succeeds, and ends, as soon as the task’s success check of RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026) holds after a step; otherwise, including when the policy stops early, it counts as a failure. The task score is the test success rate SRt=15​∑e𝟙​[successt,e]\mathrm{SR}_{t}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{e}\mathbb{1}[\text{success}_{t,e}] and the suite score 18​∑tSRt\frac{1}{8}\sum_{t}\mathrm{SR}_{t}, a task without a run counting as zero.

  • Prior work. RoboCasa365 trains and benchmarks generalist policies, evaluating in target kitchens separate from the pretraining ones (Nasiriany et al., 2026). Galbot Team et al. (2026) evaluate GPT-6 Astra as a direct and hybrid policy on it, and Kuroki et al. (2026) optimize closed-loop control code, raising success on four RoboCasa source tasks from 28.3% to 64.2% and reaching 57.0% on nine transfer tasks.

Active Search

  • Purpose. Active visual search: a humanoid robot that sees part of a 360-degree scene turns its head to find a named object (object search) or the direction to move in (path search), with as few movements as possible; most targets start out of view.

  • Source and construction. H*Bench (Yu et al., 2026a) annotates search tasks on real panoramas of transport hubs, shops and streets: an instruction, a target yaw range (and, for objects, a pitch range), and starting directions and difficulty levels; its public benchmark split has 2,400 object-search and 1,600 path-search episodes. Development and validation come from it: each task becomes one episode, with one start drawn by a fixed seed from its annotated starts; each panorama yields at most one episode, so the splits share no scene; both are stratified by search kind and difficulty in proportion to H*Bench. Development has 80 episodes (40 object, 40 path) and validation 100 (50 and 50). The test split uses the non-public in-the-wild panoramas of Imagining in 360∘ (Zhang et al., 2026d), eight from Google Street View and seven generated by image models. A target was annotated by clicking its center (objects, widened by ±30∘\pm 30^{\circ} in yaw and ±20∘\pm 20^{\circ} in pitch) or the direction to move in (±10∘\pm 10^{\circ}), with starts at multiples of 90∘90^{\circ}; one start per task gives 47 episodes (33 object, 14 path) in 15 scenes. The agent sees the development episodes with their annotations and panoramas.

  • Setting. The solution receives the instruction and a 100-degree view (960×720960\times 720 pixels), never the panorama. With at most ten actions it rotates the head by a relative angle or submits an absolute direction, which ends the episode; no submission fails. As in H*Bench, success requires the submitted direction to lie in the target ranges widened to at least the tolerances above. Up to 20 model calls per episode on average and open models on one GPU are allowed; other H*Bench data are not.

  • Starter solution. The H*Bench baseline with its prompts: one model call per step on the whole conversation (every view with the environment’s feedback), answered with one rotation or submission.

  • Metric. Success weighted by path length (SPL) (Anderson et al., 2018), counting actions: episode ee scores se​ℓe/max⁡(ℓe,pe)s_{e}\,\ell_{e}/\max(\ell_{e},p_{e}), with se∈{0,1}s_{e}\in\{0,1\} success, pep_{e} the actions taken (including the submission), and ℓe\ell_{e} the fewest that can succeed (1 if the target center lies within 50∘50^{\circ} of the starting yaw, else 2). Scores are averaged within each search kind, and the two averages are averaged.

  • Prior work. H*Bench reports about 30% success for the best proprietary models; post-training Qwen2.5-VL-3B (HVS-3B) with supervised fine-tuning and multi-turn reinforcement learning raises success from 14.83% to 47.38% (objects) and from 6.44% to 24.94% (paths) (Yu et al., 2026a). Imagining in 360∘ adds an Imaginator that predicts the layout of seen and unseen regions for a frozen actor, raising HVS-3B from 48.04% to 62.75% and from 24.12% to 39.38% on H*Bench (Zhang et al., 2026d).

RoboLab

  • Purpose. Whether the agent can obtain one tabletop manipulation policy that follows instructions for tasks it has never seen; the splits contain different tasks, so the score measures generalization across tasks.

  • Source and construction. The pool is every RoboLab-120 (Yang et al., 2026a) task of difficulty simple or moderate with a horizon of at most 60 s (73 tasks). Each task is given one group of RoboLab’s taxonomy: procedural (affordance, reorientation, sorting, stacking), else relational (conjunction, counting, spatial), else visual (color, semantics, size). Tasks are shuffled within each (group, difficulty) stratum with a fixed seed and dealt by systematic sampling to development (16 tasks), validation (12), test (24), and an unused remainder, so every split has each stratum in proportion; test has 4 procedural, 9 relational, 10 visual, and 1 unattributed task. Development tasks include stacking bowls, packing cans into a bin, standing a jug upright, and selecting a hammer by color. Each task keeps its RoboLab scene, default instruction, horizon, success predicate, and subtask tracker unchanged. Start states are deterministic, so a task’s episodes differ only through the policy; development runs one episode per task, validation and test two (16, 24, and 48 episodes). The agent sees development tasks and results, validation aggregates only, and no held-out task names.

  • Setting. The DROID setup, a Franka Panda arm with a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper, in Isaac Lab at 15 Hz. The policy receives the instruction, over-the-shoulder and wrist RGB images, over-the-shoulder depth, calibration, and proprioception, never the task name or object poses, and returns chunks of absolute end-effector poses and gripper commands, limited to 5 cm and 0.25 rad per step. It may call the run’s model at most 40 times within 1200 s of thinking per episode, no other model, and may not key behavior on task identity.

  • Starter solution. One model call per gripper waypoint, given both images, the pose, and calibration, followed by a straight-line move and an open or close.

  • Metric. RoboLab’s total score (Yang et al., 2026a), Score=100N​∑e=1N(𝟙​[successe]+(1−𝟙​[successe])​qe)\mathrm{Score}=\frac{100}{N}\sum_{e=1}^{N}\bigl(\mathbb{1}[\text{success}_{e}]+(1-\mathbb{1}[\text{success}_{e}])\,q_{e}\bigr) over the N=48N=48 test episodes, where qe∈[0,1]q_{e}\in[0,1] is the fraction of subtasks completed when the episode ends. The success rate is also reported.

  • Prior work. RoboLab analyses task-generalist policies along visual, procedural, and relational competencies (Yang et al., 2026a). Chen et al. (2026c) evaluate agents without a trained policy on its 120 tasks with vague instructions: code-as-policy (CaP-X) reaches 14.4% success, VLM-based task and motion planning (TiPToP) 18.9%, and their orchestrator without a vision–language–action policy 17.8%.

LIBERO-MAX

  • Purpose. Whether the agent can build a robot controller that adapts when the world changes during execution, not only before it starts.

  • Source and construction. LIBERO-MAX (Zhang et al., 2026e) has 8,000 paired cases on LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) scenes, with starting configurations from LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025) and LIBERO-PRO (Zhou et al., 2025). A case pairs a Base episode with a Dynamic episode that has the same start and policy seed and receives one online event: target or receptacle relocation, camera shift, sensor-noise onset, illumination or visual-theme switch, a burst of distractors, or an inserted obstacle. In the selected cases the event fires when the robot comes within 0.18 m of a designated object, before the grasp. Cases are selected from official metadata, never from outcomes. All splits use three LIBERO tasks (a bowl from a drawer onto a plate, a sauce bottle into a basket, a plate pushed to the front of a stove) and the same number of cases per event type: 8, 16 and 24 pairs for development, validation and test. No initial physical state appears in two splits, and states used in earlier experiments are excluded from validation and test. The agent sees the development case definitions.

  • Setting. A simulated Franka Panda (MuJoCo). Each step, the solution receives RGB and metric depth from an external and a wrist camera, their calibration, the robot state and the instruction, and returns an absolute end-effector pose and gripper command. It may query a frozen X-VLA policy (Zheng et al., 2025) for 30-step action chunks, possibly on transformed images, and call the model up to 16 times per episode; no other model, no training, no simulator state. The Dynamic episode replays the Base episode exactly until the event.

  • Starter solution. Executes the X-VLA chunks unchanged, without calling the model.

  • Metric. Dynamic success rate 1P​∑p=1Pspdyn\frac{1}{P}\sum_{p=1}^{P}s^{\mathrm{dyn}}_{p} over all PP planned pairs, with spdyn∈{0,1}s^{\mathrm{dyn}}_{p}\in\{0,1\} the LIBERO success check of the Dynamic episode; an episode that reaches the horizon or its 20-minute limit unsolved fails. The Base success rate and the paired difference, as in LIBERO-MAX, are also reported.

  • Prior work. Across fourteen vision–language–action, hybrid and world-action policies, LIBERO-MAX events lower success by 11.0 to 25.7 percentage points, mostly through geometry and observation changes (Zhang et al., 2026e).

LIBERO-PRO

  • Purpose. Whether the agent can build a robot controller that stays successful when a familiar task is perturbed before the episode starts, rather than relying on the conditions the underlying policy was trained under.

  • Source and construction. LIBERO-PRO (Zhou et al., 2025) perturbs LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) tasks in their objects, initial states, instructions and environments, and releases the perturbed task definitions and initial states. Ten of its categories are used: object appearance, object shape, object texture, object positions, paraphrased instruction, changed task goal, camera view angle, initial robot pose, visual noise or glare, and view occlusion. Each case is one perturbed initial state of one of the three LIBERO tasks of LIBERO-MAX. Cases are selected from official metadata, with equal numbers per category in each split, spread over the three tasks: 10, 20 and 30 episodes for development, validation and test (ten per task in test). No initial physical state appears in two splits or in LIBERO-MAX, and states used in earlier experiments are excluded from validation and test. The agent sees the development case definitions.

  • Setting. As in LIBERO-MAX: a controller that may query the frozen X-VLA policy (Zheng et al., 2025) and call the model up to 16 times per episode, with a 20-minute limit per episode and no other model.

  • Starter solution. Executes the X-VLA chunks unchanged, without calling the model.

  • Metric. Success rate 1N​∑i=1Nsi\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}s_{i} over all NN planned episodes, with sis_{i} the native LIBERO success check; an episode that reaches the horizon or the time limit unsolved fails.

  • Prior work. LIBERO-PRO reports that models above 90% success under the standard LIBERO evaluation fall to 0.0% under its generalized setting, a sign of memorized training conditions (Zhou et al., 2025). LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025) analyses robustness along seven dimensions: object layout, camera viewpoint, initial robot state, language, lighting, background texture and sensor noise.

Embodied-SWE

  • Purpose. Whether the agent can write, offline with a simulator, a control program for a long-horizon, contact-rich tool-use task that then runs without any model.

  • Source and construction. The spatula task of EmbodiedSWE-Bench (Shen et al., 2026b): a Franka arm under operational-space control in Isaac Lab wedges a spatula under a slice of bread in a pan, flips it, reloads it onto the blade and serves it flat onto a plate, touching the bread only with the tool. The environment is built with the benchmark’s tools in its setting without agent tools, and the grader is withheld. Each evaluation runs eight parallel environments with random bread size and pose, plate position and spatula pose. Development uses the build seed (8 trajectories); validation 2 and test 4 hidden random seeds (16 and 32 trajectories). The agent receives the benchmark’s task statement, its rule for batched solutions and its staged-planning guide.

  • Setting. A program that commands the robot only through the environment’s step function and may read object poses. Writing simulator state, applying external forces, changing physics or the scene, or altering the grader scores zero. A rollout has 30 minutes of wall time, and no model is called during evaluation. During development the agent has full simulator access on one GPU.

  • Starter solution. Holds the arm still for ten steps and scores zero.

  • Metric. The EmbodiedSWE-Bench rubric score (Shen et al., 2026b): each trajectory receives the credit of the furthest stage it reaches, namely spatula lifted (0.2), bread on the blade (0.4), bread flipped and flat (0.6), bread carried on the blade (0.8) and bread on the plate (1.0). The score is the mean over all trajectories of the split; a crashed rollout scores zero, and a timed-out one is scored as it stands. The final-state success rate is also reported.

  • Prior work. EmbodiedSWE-Bench (Shen et al., 2026b) evaluates coding agents that write such programs in one four-hour run per task, and uses their solutions to generate demonstrations for vision–language–action models. On this task, single runs of frontier coding agents reach rubric scores from 0.2 to 1.0, with one run disqualified for reward hacking.

A.2  Reasoning

Ego-Exo Memory

  • Purpose. Memory reasoning across two synchronized views of one activity. The evidence for an answer is visible only at particular moments, often in one view, and the model sees few frames per call, so the solution must choose which moments and views to show.

  • Source and construction. The questions are the Ego-Exo4D portion of EgoExoMem (Liu et al., 2026b): 764 human-verified four-option questions on 125 recordings of cooking and bicycle repair from Ego-Exo4D (Grauman et al., 2024). Each recording has an egocentric view from the glasses of the person performing the activity (448×448448\times 448 pixels) and an exocentric view from a fixed camera (796×448796\times 448 pixels), synchronized at 30 frames per second and lasting from 20 seconds to 23 minutes. The questions concern habitual location, instantaneous position, resulting location, egocentric direction, object state, allocentric relation, and temporal order. All recordings of one session (the same room and people) are assigned to one split, stratified by activity, with about 35%, 25%, and 40% of the questions in the development, validation, and test splits. Each split then keeps a fixed-seed sample stratified by activity and question type and spread over its videos: 80 questions on 38 videos, 80 on 33, and 120 on 47. The answer options are shuffled once and the videos are anonymized. With each development question the agent also receives the annotated moments at which the answer is visible and the view that shows it.

  • Setting. Given the question, both videos, and frames of both views at one frame per second, the solution returns an option letter. It may call the model three times per question on average over a split, with at most 16×448×44816\times 448\times 448 pixels per call; further calls are refused. It may run open-weight models, for example for frame retrieval, on one GPU, has no network access during evaluation, and may not use the annotations of EgoExoMem or Ego-Exo4D.

  • Starter solution. Shows the model eight evenly spaced frames of each view, each labeled with its view and time and downscaled so that all sixteen fit the pixel limit, followed by the question, in a single call.

  • Metric. Accuracy over the questions of a split; a question without a valid letter counts as wrong. Chance is 0.25.

  • Prior work. EgoExoMem evaluates multimodal language models on 2.6K cross-view memory questions of eight types. On the full benchmark, the best existing model reaches 55.3%, and the training-free frame selection method E2-Select, which allocates the frame budget by relevance and samples frames per view with a kk-DPP, reaches 58.2% (Liu et al., 2026b).

Kinematics

  • Purpose. Quantitative physical reasoning from video: building a measurement procedure around a fixed vision–language model, so that quantities follow from pixels, time, and a known scale.

  • Source and construction. QuantiPhy (Puyin et al., 2026) contains 3,355 questions on 569 videos from physics simulations, laboratory recordings, internet clips, and segmented objects. The task uses its public labeled validation set, 158 questions on 24 videos. Each question asks for the size, distance, velocity, or acceleration of an object, possibly at a stated time, in stated units, and gives one prior in physical units: a known length, speed, or acceleration, and for some videos depths. The videos are assigned to fixed lists, so that no video appears in two splits and every split mixes the four video sources and the static and dynamic priors and targets: 39 questions on 6 videos for development, 52 on 8 for validation, and 67 on 10 for testing.

  • Setting. The solution returns a number in the unit of the question. It does not call the model being evaluated: the only language or vision–language model it may use is Qwen3.8-27B with open weights, served locally with at most 32 images (32×640×36032\times 640\times 360 pixels in total) per call and eight calls per question on average over a split. It may add non-language vision models and classical code on one GPU, such as point trackers, optical flow, detectors, segmenters, and depth or pose estimators, but no other language model, neither in the solution nor to label data, and no network access during evaluation.

  • Starter solution. Shows the fixed model four evenly spaced frames, the question, and the prior in a single call with reasoning disabled, and reads the first number of the reply.

  • Metric. The mean relative accuracy (MRA). For a prediction y^i\hat{y}_{i} of the true value yiy_{i},

    MRA=1N∑i=1N1|𝒞|∑θ∈𝒞[|y^i−yi||yi|<1−θ],𝒞={0.1,0.2,…,0.9,0.95},\mathrm{MRA}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|}\sum_{\theta\in\mathcal{C}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\frac{|\hat{y}_{i}-y_{i}|}{|y_{i}|}<1-\theta\right],\qquad\mathcal{C}=\{0.1,0.2,\dots,0.9,0.95\},

    and a question without a numeric answer scores zero. MRA was introduced by VSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025) with thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95; the threshold set above is that of QuantiPhy (Puyin et al., 2026).

  • Prior work. QuantiPhy evaluates 21 vision–language models that answer directly from the video. The best reaches an MRA of 53.1, below the average human score of 55.6; the models rely on pretrained world knowledge more than on the given video and prior, and a four-step chain of thought (measure the source property in pixels, estimate the scale, measure the target in pixels, convert) lowers the score of 19 of the 21 models (Puyin et al., 2026).

Mass

  • Purpose. Estimating a property that is not directly visible: weight depends on material, on whether an object is solid or hollow, and on how its volume is filled.

  • Source and construction. The items are product listings of Amazon Berkeley Objects (Collins et al., 2022) that state a weight, all three dimensions, and a main photograph. Consumables (food, supplements, cleaning and medical supplies) and multipacks or sets, recognized by name, are removed, as are items outside 10 g to 150 kg and items whose weight divided by the volume of their bounding box lies outside 5 to 5000 kg/m3, which removes unit and listing errors. Variants of one product (the same brand and the same first six words of the name) form one group, and one item per group is drawn with a fixed seed. The groups are split into 300 development, 300 validation, and 600 test items, with at most 3% of a split from one product type, giving about 130 product types per split. Each item keeps its main photograph and up to two others, with the longer side at most 1024 pixels.

  • Setting. Given the photographs, a coarse product type, and the listed dimensions in centimetres, but not the name, brand, or description, the solution states the weight in kilograms. As in Kinematics, the only language or vision–language model is the fixed Qwen3.8-27B, with at most eight images (8×1024×10248\times 1024\times 1024 pixels) per call and four calls per item on average. Non-language models such as segmenters, depth estimators, image encoders, and regressors trained on the development split may run on one GPU; other language models, text encoders applied to other data, and any external source of the weights are not allowed.

  • Starter solution. Shows the fixed model the main photograph, the product type, and the dimensions in a single call with reasoning disabled, and reads the first number of the reply.

  • Metric. The mean relative accuracy with the thresholds of Kinematics, averaged over items; an item without a numeric answer scores zero.

  • Prior work. Image2mass (Standley et al., 2017) collected about 150,000 online product listings with images, sizes, and weights, and estimates mass from an image together with the object’s dimensions, comparing learned models with human estimates. Amazon Berkeley Objects (Collins et al., 2022) provides catalogue images, metadata, and 3D models of real products for object understanding.

ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2

  • Purpose. Abstract reasoning from few examples: inferring a grid transformation from a few demonstration pairs and applying it to new inputs, on puzzles designed to require little prior knowledge.

  • Source and construction. The puzzles come from the official public repositories at fixed versions: 400 training and 400 evaluation puzzles for ARC-AGI-1 (Chollet, 2019), and 1000 training and 120 evaluation puzzles for ARC-AGI-2 (Chollet et al., 2025). Each puzzle has demonstration pairs and one or more test inputs; grids are at most 30×3030\times 30 with ten colors. Training puzzles identical to an evaluation puzzle are removed (one for ARC-AGI-1). The remaining training puzzles are ordered by a seeded hash: the first 80 form the validation split, and the rest form the development pool, which the agent receives with answers (319 puzzles for ARC-AGI-1); a fixed panel of 32 development puzzles is scored in development evaluations. The test split consists of all official evaluation puzzles, 400 for ARC-AGI-1 and 120 for ARC-AGI-2, so validation and test puzzles are disjoint.

  • Setting. Given the demonstration pairs and the test inputs, the solution returns at most two candidate grids per test input. It may call the model up to 2000 times per evaluation, with four puzzles solved in parallel in independent sessions, and runs in a sandbox without a GPU or network access. It may use program search, hand-written rules, or models trained on the development puzzles, but may not obtain or store held-out answers. Invalid predictions score zero.

  • Starter solution. Asks the model for two candidate outputs as JSON in a single call per puzzle; an unparseable reply counts as no answer.

  • Metric. Pass@2, in percent: with gi​j1,gi​j2g_{ij}^{1},g_{ij}^{2} the two candidates for test input jj of puzzle ii,

    pass@2=100N∑i=1N∏j[yi​j∈{gi​j1,gi​j2}],\text{pass@2}=\frac{100}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j}\mathbf{1}\!\left[y_{ij}\in\{g_{ij}^{1},g_{ij}^{2}\}\right],

    so a puzzle counts only when every test output is matched exactly. The two attempts per test input follow the ARC Prize protocol (Chollet et al., 2024).

  • Prior work. ARC (Chollet, 2019) was proposed to measure the efficiency of skill acquisition on novel problems. In ARC Prize 2024 the best private-set score rose from 33% to 55.5%, mainly through deep-learning-guided program synthesis and test-time training (Chollet et al., 2024); test-time training brings an 8B language model to 53.0% on the public validation set, and 61.9% when ensembled with program synthesis (Akyürek et al., 2024). ARC-AGI-2 raises the difficulty: on its semi-private set, o3 (medium) scores 3.0%, against 53.0% on ARC-AGI-1 (Chollet et al., 2025).

ARC-AGI-3

  • Purpose. Learning an interactive environment without instructions: finding out by acting what the controls do and what completes a level, then completing levels with few actions.

  • Source and construction. ARC-AGI-3 (ARC Prize Foundation, 2026) consists of turn-based games on grids of up to 64×6464\times 64 cells with 16 colors, each with several levels and a human baseline action count per level. Its public set has 25 games, and official scores use 110 further private games. The task uses the 25 public games at a fixed version of the official toolkit, split by game with a seeded hash into 10 development, 5 validation, and 10 test games. The agent sees only the identifiers of the development games and plays them through the interface; the game code, the human baselines, and the validation and test games are not accessible to it.

  • Setting. The solution observes the current frame, the available actions, and the number of completed levels, and submits actions: directions, a game-specific action, a click at a grid position, and undo, whose effects must be inferred; a reset is allowed only after the game is lost. Each game allows at most 1000 actions, 120 model calls, and 1200 seconds, and each evaluation at most 1200 model calls. Games are played one at a time, each from a fresh start with a fixed seed, and no memory or files carry over between games. The solution may not contain game solutions or game code.

  • Starter solution. Sends the model the current frame as an image and as rows of color values, a short memory, and the recent actions, and executes up to eight actions returned per call along with an updated memory.

  • Metric. Relative human action efficiency (RHAE), computed by the official toolkit. With hℓh_{\ell} the human baseline and aℓa_{\ell} the agent’s actions on level ℓ\ell, a completed level scores Sℓ=min⁡(1.15,hℓ/aℓ)2S_{\ell}=\min(1.15,\,h_{\ell}/a_{\ell})^{2} and an uncompleted level zero; with weights wℓ=ℓw_{\ell}=\ell over the nn levels of a game of which kk are completed,

    E=min⁡(∑ℓ=1kwℓ∑ℓ=1nwℓ,∑ℓ=1nwℓ​Sℓ∑ℓ=1nwℓ),E=\min\!\left(\frac{\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}w_{\ell}}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}w_{\ell}},\;\frac{\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}w_{\ell}S_{\ell}}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}w_{\ell}}\right),

    and the score is the mean of EE over games, multiplied by 100 (ARC Prize Foundation, 2026). A game stopped by a limit keeps its partial score.

  • Prior work. ARC-AGI-3 (ARC Prize Foundation, 2026) reports that humans solve all of its environments, while frontier AI systems scored below 1% as of March 2026; in its preview competition, the best entry, which trains a convolutional network with reinforcement learning to predict which actions change the frame, scored 12.58%.

Spatial-VSI

  • Purpose. Spatial reasoning about indoor scenes from a moving camera: counts, metric sizes and distances, relative directions, routes, and the order of appearance.

  • Source and construction. VSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025) contains over 5000 questions on 288 videos of real rooms from ScanNet, ScanNet++, and ARKitScenes (Dai et al., 2017; Yeshwanth et al., 2023; Baruch et al., 2021). It has ten question types in eight groups: object counting, absolute distance, object size, and room size, answered by numbers, and relative distance, relative direction (easy, medium, hard), route planning, and appearance order, answered by option letters. The scenes of a fixed dataset version are shuffled with a fixed seed and dealt to the test, validation, and development splits in proportions 40%, 30%, and 30%; each split then keeps questions stratified so that the eight groups are weighted as in the official score. The splits hold 80 questions from 46 scenes for development, 480 from 84 scenes for validation, and 320 from 100 scenes for testing.

  • Setting. Given the video (640 by 480 pixels, one to three minutes), the question, and the options, the solution returns an answer. It may call the model twice per question on average over a split and uses no other model and no downloaded weights; its own code, such as geometry and classical vision with OpenCV, is allowed. It may not read the annotations of the source datasets or access the network, has no GPU, and has four hours per evaluation.

  • Starter solution. Shows the model 16 evenly spaced frames, 512 pixels wide, with the official VSI-Bench prompt, in one call per question.

  • Metric. The overall score of VSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025). A multiple-choice answer is correct when its first word is the option letter; a numerical answer receives the mean relative accuracy with thresholds {0.50,0.55,…,0.95}\{0.50,0.55,\dots,0.95\} and the condition |y^−y|/y≤1−θ|\hat{y}-y|/y\leq 1-\theta, and zero if it is not a number. Scores are averaged within each group, the three direction levels are first averaged into one, and the eight groups are averaged, giving a value between 0 and 1.

  • Prior work. VSI-Bench finds that the best model it tests, Gemini-1.5 Pro, averages 45.4%, against about 79% for humans on a subset; chain-of-thought, self-consistency, and tree-of-thoughts prompting do not help, whereas asking the model to draw a cognitive map raises relative-distance accuracy from 46.0% to 56.0% (Yang et al., 2025). VSI-Bench-Debiased removes questions that can be answered without the video (Brown et al., 2025), and Spatial-MLLM adds a 3D spatial encoder initialized from a visual geometry model to a multimodal language model (Wu et al., 2025b).

A.3  Creation

Image Editing

  • Purpose. Whether the agent can build an instruction-based image editor that performs the edit requested in English or Chinese while leaving the rest of the photograph intact, across local, global, text, retouching and restoration, reasoning, and compound edits. The editing model is not prescribed: choosing, combining, and adapting open models is part of the task.

  • Source and construction. The evaluation set was built for this task in two versions. The first has 100 images; the second, used here, adds 86 images and 14 restoration photographs, for 200 images. The 186 photographs, paintings, and illustrations are CC0 or public-domain works from Wikimedia Commons, each checked for its licence and excluding identifiable people, minors, trademarks, and third-party works; two images of puzzles (an arithmetic problem on a blackboard and a number sequence) were made for the task, and four images carry a reproducible synthetic degradation (blur, color cast, or low contrast) to be undone. The 14 restoration photographs show haze, fog, smoke, lens flare, reflections on glass, or cast shadows; all come from the data of UniSER (Zhang et al., 2025c), including ten of its 39 in-the-wild evaluation images and three of its paired images from NH-HAZE (Ancuti et al., 2020), FlareReal600, and WSRD+ (Vasluianu et al., 2023). Images are resized to at most 1536×10241536\times 1024 pixels with sides that are multiples of 16, and span outdoor (85), product (34), indoor (32), low-quality (21), illustration (13), text (11), and document (4) images. Each image has one instruction, written in Chinese (106) or English (94) together with a translation into the other language, and is assigned to one of 23 kinds of edit in six families: local semantic edits, namely adding, removing, or replacing an object, changing its attributes, changing a pose, setting a count, or moving objects (71 images); global edits of style, background, or lighting, weather, and season (30); text editing, namely replacing, writing, or editing Chinese text (22); retouching and restoration, namely tone, old or degraded photographs and soft effects, removal of clutter, and outpainting to a new aspect ratio (34); edits that require inference, such as candles after three hours of burning, the farthest of several glasses, leaves in late autumn, or a completed sudoku (25); and compound or constrained instructions (18). Each sample is labeled with a difficulty (44, 114, and 42 at three levels) and the size of the edited region (small, medium, large, or global), and is annotated for scoring: a mask of the region allowed to change (92 images), objects that must appear (43) or disappear (32), a target count (11), text that must be readable (24) or gone (14), a target aspect ratio (5), content that must be kept (74), the parts of a compound instruction (13), and a description of the intended result of an inference edit (31). The images are divided into 50 development, 70 validation, and 80 test images, stratified by kind of edit. The development samples come with their annotations, and their evaluations return per-sample judge rationales and side-by-side comparisons; validation and test return only the aggregate score.

  • Setting. The solution is an editing program that receives the image, the instruction, and its language, and writes an image at the input size. It may use any open-weight editing or generation model, several models at once, vision models, classical image processing, and its own fine-tuning on the development split; Qwen-Image-2.1, Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 with distilled few-step adapters (Wu et al., 2025a), and HunyuanImage-3.0-Instruct (Tencent Hunyuan Foundation Model Team, 2025) are provided. It may not use the judge’s model family, remote services, or the annotations. Evaluation runs offline on four 80 GB GPUs with, on average, 150 s per image per GPU; the solution does not call the model being evaluated.

  • Starter solution. Qwen-Image-Edit-2509 with an eight-step distilled adapter, given the instruction unchanged, producing one output per image.

  • Metric. A frozen judge, GLM-4.5V (GLM-V Team, 2025) at temperature 0, sees the source and the output and rates instruction compliance SC\mathrm{SC} and preservation PR\mathrm{PR}, and, from the output alone, perceptual quality PQ\mathrm{PQ}, each from 0 to 10. The preservation rubric depends on the kind of edit (for example, only content and composition for style transfer, only the kept subjects for a background change), and the judge is told the annotated parts, the kept content, and, for inference edits, the intended result. Global deformation is measured rather than judged: a SIFT (Lowe, 2004) and RANSAC (Fischler and Bolles, 1981) homography from input to output gives the 90th-percentile displacement p90p_{90} in pixels at a 512-pixel short side, g=exp(−max(0,p90−0.5)/6)g=\exp(-\max(0,p_{90}-0.5)/6), and PR′=max⁡(0,PR−5​(1−g))\mathrm{PR}^{\prime}=\max(0,\mathrm{PR}-5(1-g)). The judge score is J=110​SC⋅PQ​(0.5+0.05​PR′)J=\tfrac{1}{10}\sqrt{\mathrm{SC}\cdot\mathrm{PQ}}\,(0.5+0.05\,\mathrm{PR}^{\prime}). The programmatic score PP averages the checks that apply: object presence and absence and the exact count, answered by the judge; for text, one minus the lowest character error rate over two OCR readings and the judge’s transcription, and the absence of text to be removed; the aspect ratio of outpainted images, max⁡(0,1−5​|r/r∗−1|)\max(0,1-5|r/r^{\ast}-1|); preservation, clip⁡(1−(MAD−0.02)/0.10)\mathrm{clip}(1-(\mathrm{MAD}-0.02)/0.10) from the mean absolute color difference outside the dilated edit region after alignment; and detail, clip⁡((c​s−0.55)/0.40)\mathrm{clip}((cs-0.55)/0.40) from the contrast–structure term of SSIM (Wang et al., 2004) at a 1024-pixel short side. Without a mask, the edit region is formed from the judge’s boxes of the edited objects. A sample scores 0.5​J+0.5​P0.5J+0.5P (JJ if no check applies), and 0 if SC<3\mathrm{SC}<3 or no image is produced. The score is the mean of the six family means, in [0,1][0,1].

  • Prior work. GEdit-Bench, introduced with the Step1X-Edit editor (Liu et al., 2025), evaluates instruction-based editing on real user requests with a vision–language judge of semantic consistency and perceptual quality, which VIEScore (Ku et al., 2024) combines as SC⋅PQ\sqrt{\mathrm{SC}\cdot\mathrm{PQ}}; the judge score above takes this form and adds the preservation term and the programmatic checks. UniSER (Zhang et al., 2025c) removes soft effects such as haze, flare, shadows, and reflections with a single diffusion model and evaluates its in-the-wild images, which lack ground truth, with reference-free metrics and a vision–language judge.

Multi-turn Editing

  • Purpose. Whether the agent can improve a multi-turn editing system, in which each instruction is applied to the previous result and becomes known only at its turn, so that errors in content and image quality accumulate over the session.

  • Source and construction. All 100 sessions of MSE-Bench, the multi-turn editing benchmark introduced with VINCIE (Qu et al., 2026), at a fixed revision. Each session is a real photograph, used unchanged at its original size (many are small), and five instructions that add, remove, or replace objects, change attributes, backgrounds, posture, expression, orientation, position, actions, or interactions, restyle the image, or move the camera (dolly, pan, tilt, orbit); MSE-Bench labels 20 operation types. The sessions are split into 30 development, 30 validation, and 40 test sessions by a seeded search that balances the per-turn counts of the 20 operation types, the sessions with a camera operation, and the images under 512 pixels on the short side. For the development sessions the agent also sees the MSE-Bench annotations (operation types and descriptions of the intended results); the solution never receives them.

  • Setting. The solution is a session object that is reset with the source image and returns one image per instruction; it may keep earlier images and instructions. The editing model is fixed to the original Qwen-Image-Edit (August 2025) (Wu et al., 2025a) with its four- and eight-step distilled adapters, since the later 2509 and 2511 releases degrade into blocky noise when edited repeatedly. Prompt rewriting, sampler settings, candidate selection, masking and compositing, and Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Bai et al., 2025b) as a helper are allowed; training the editing model, network access, and any copy of MSE-Bench or of VINCIE’s outputs are not. Each of four GPUs runs one process with 300 s of start-up and, on average, 60 s per turn. A failed turn, an aspect-ratio change above 5%, or a timeout scores 0 for that turn and the rest of the session. The solution does not call the model being evaluated.

  • Starter solution. Edits the previous image with each turn’s instruction, using the eight-step adapter and a fixed seed.

  • Metric. Each turn kk is judged by a frozen GLM-4.5V (GLM-V Team, 2025) at about one megapixel. Given the instructions of turns 1..k1..k and the images up to turn kk, MSE-Bench’s own evaluation prompt rates prompt following PF\mathrm{PF} and consistency CONS\mathrm{CONS} with the previous image; a strict prompt rates the perceptual quality PQ\mathrm{PQ} of the turn’s image alone (all 0–10). The turn score is 110​PF⋅PQ​(0.5+0.05​CONS)\tfrac{1}{10}\sqrt{\mathrm{PF}\cdot\mathrm{PQ}}\,(0.5+0.05\,\mathrm{CONS}), or 0 if PF<3\mathrm{PF}<3; the score averages over the five turns and then over sessions. MSE-Bench’s cumulative success rate, the fraction of sessions in which every turn up to kk has PF>6\mathrm{PF}>6 and CONS>6\mathrm{CONS}>6, is reported for k=1,3,5k=1,3,5.

  • Prior work. VINCIE (Qu et al., 2026) learns in-context image editing from video and introduced MSE-Bench to measure multi-turn editing by the success rate at each turn, judged by GPT-4o. Here the editing model is fixed and the agent improves the system around it.

Video Generation

  • Purpose. Whether the agent can build an executable text-to-video workflow around a frozen video generator, deciding how to plan prompts, spend a fixed generation budget, inspect frames, and select candidates, so that the videos follow compositional prompts.

  • Source and construction. The prompts come from T2V-CompBench (Sun et al., 2025), at a fixed revision of its prompt lists, restricted to four of its seven categories: consistent attribute binding, action binding, generative numeracy, and spatial relationships (two-dimensional only). Each split has 20 prompts, five per category. Near-duplicate prompts were grouped into families (connected components of normalized token Jaccard similarity of at least 0.65); the validation and test prompts were drawn in a salted hash order, excluding the families of development prompts and taking at most one prompt per family. The agent sees the development prompts and their scores; validation and test prompts are private.

  • Setting. The generator is MiniMax H3 (MiniMax, 2026b) with frozen weights, producing 124 frames at 864×480864\times 480 and 24 frames per second. For each prompt the workflow may make at most three generation requests totalling 50 denoising steps, choosing prompts, seeds, step counts, and flow shift; sample frames; call the model being evaluated at most twice (40 calls per evaluation), with images; and process videos locally. It returns one video. It has no network, no direct GPU access, and no access to the evaluators, and may not add text or cues aimed at the evaluators. Each evaluation runs on one 80 GB H100 within 150 minutes; prompts unfinished when the workflow time runs out score 0.

  • Starter solution. A single generation request with the prompt unchanged and the default seed, 50 steps, and flow shift.

  • Metric. The original T2V-CompBench evaluators score each video against the original prompt with their default prompts, thresholds, and seeds: attribute binding and action binding with the multimodal-LLM evaluation using LLaVA-v1.6-34B (Liu et al., 2024a) on sampled frames, and numeracy and spatial relationships with the detection-based evaluation using Grounding DINO (Liu et al., 2024b) (16 sampled frames, six of them in a grid for the language model). Each video scores in [0,1][0,1], a missing or corrupt video scores 0, and the score is the mean of the four category means. Because of the subset and the fixed resolution, the scores are not comparable with the T2V-CompBench leaderboard.

  • Prior work. T2V-CompBench (Sun et al., 2025) benchmarks text-to-video models on 1,400 prompts in seven compositional categories, with multimodal-LLM-based, detection-based, and tracking-based metrics validated against human judgments. Here the generator is fixed, and the agent improves the workflow around it.

Text-to-Image

  • Purpose. Whether the agent can make a text-to-image program satisfy every constraint of new prompts in Chinese and English while keeping image quality, either with a fixed generator or with any open model.

  • Source and construction. The 200 prompts and their rubrics were written for this task: 100 in Chinese and 100 in English (not translations of each other), ten in each of 20 subcategories of six categories: subjects and attributes (identity, color, material), counting and binding (single and multiple classes, attribute binding, excluded content), spatial relations and interaction (position, depth and containment, actions and roles), text and layout (English, Chinese, multiple text blocks), style and presentation (medium, lighting and season, camera and composition), and reasoning and composition (world knowledge, causality and time, logical quantity, multiple constraints). Each subcategory has two easy, five medium, and three hard prompts by the author’s judgment. Each prompt has a fixed seed and size (1024×10241024\times 1024 for 145 prompts, 1280×7681280\times 768 or 768×1280768\times 1280 for 55) and a rubric of atomic criteria (954 in total) of four types: semantic, count, absence, and exact text, the latter copied verbatim from the prompt; each requirement is credited once. After authoring, every prompt and rubric was reviewed for physical consistency, count logic, text literals, coverage, and duplicate credit, which revised 32 prompts, 51 rubrics, and 34 sizes; scripts check quotas, uniqueness, field consistency, and split isolation, and flagged cross-split pairs of similar wording were reviewed by hand. The prompts are split into 50 development, 70 validation, and 80 test prompts by semantic group (178 groups of prompts sharing a central scene), each split half Chinese and half English with 20/50/30% easy, medium, and hard prompts. Development prompts come with rubrics and per-image feedback; validation returns only the score.

  • Setting. The solution receives a prompt, its language, size, and seed, and writes one image. With the fixed generator, all images come from the frozen Qwen-Image-2.1 (Wu et al., 2025a); prompt rewriting, layout planning, sampling settings, several candidates with selection, Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Bai et al., 2025b) as a helper, and ordinary image tools are allowed, but no training or adapters. With any model, other open-weight generators, routing, and training on the development split are also allowed. Neither may use the judge’s model family, the rubrics, the network, or hosted models at evaluation, which runs on four GPUs with at most 600 s per image.

  • Starter solution. One image from Qwen-Image-2.1 with the prompt unchanged and 40 sampling steps.

  • Metric. A frozen GLM-4.5V (GLM-V Team, 2025) judges each image: a semantic criterion scores 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, or 1; a count, absence, or exact-text criterion scores 0 or 1; and the quality Q∈[0,1]Q\in[0,1] rates rendering defects, excluding prompt compliance and intended style. With criterion scores cic_{i} and weights wiw_{i} (all 1), C=∑iwi​ci/∑iwiC=\sum_{i}w_{i}c_{i}/\sum_{i}w_{i} and the image scores C⁡(0.5+0.5​Q)C\,(0.5+0.5\,Q); a missing or wrongly sized image scores 0. Scores are averaged within each category and then over the six categories. The reported score is the mean of the test scores of the two settings.

  • Prior work. GenEval (Ghosh et al., 2023) and T2I-CompBench (Huang et al., 2023a) evaluate compositional text-to-image generation with detectors and other vision models. The prompts here are new and these benchmarks’ scores are not reproduced.

A.4  Reconstruction

3D Tracking

  • Purpose. Whether the agent can assemble a system that segments every object in a few widely separated views of an indoor scene and gives each object the same identity in every view, from RGB images alone. Without camera poses or depth, the views must be associated through appearance and implicit geometry: the cross-view instance tracking that IGGT (Li et al., 2026) introduced as an evaluation of instance-grounded 3D reconstruction.

  • Source and construction. The validation and test clips are the 3D tracking benchmark released with IGGT, which samples a few views per scene from ScanNet (Dai et al., 2017) and ScanNet++ (Yeshwanth et al., 2023) for spatial coverage with sufficient overlap and annotates a subset of objects by hand with identities consistent across views. Each clip has six to nine RGB views, resized to 592×448592\times 448 pixels, typically with four to eight annotated objects such as furniture, lamps, and decorations; walls, floors, and ceilings are not annotated. The 8 ScanNet++ clips form the validation split and the 10 ScanNet clips the test split. The development split consists of 100 clips built from ScanNet++ training scenes that share no scene with the validation clips: eight views are drawn from a random stretch covering 30 to 80% of a capture, and up to eight object-like instances are kept (visible in at least two views, at most a quarter of any view, and at least 0.1% of the clip’s pixels); a clip with fewer than four is drawn again. The agent sees the development views with their instance maps.

  • Setting. The solution is a program that receives the views of one clip and returns one instance map per view, with 0 for the background and identities consistent across views. It may use any publicly released pretrained model or library and needs no training; it does not call the model being evaluated. It runs on one GPU without network access, and a whole split must finish within 45 minutes.

  • Starter solution. Clusters the colors of each view into six clusters with kk-means, splits them into connected regions covering 0.2 to 20% of the image, and links each region to the existing track with the nearest mean color, or starts a new track.

  • Metric. Evaluation is class-agnostic. Predicted and annotated tracks are matched one to one, greedily in decreasing order of their temporal IoU, which accumulates intersection and union over the views: for an annotated object with masks GfG_{f} and its matched prediction PfP_{f} in views f=1,…,Sf=1,\dots,S,

    T​-​IoU=∑f|Pf∩Gf|∑f|Pf∪Gf|.\mathrm{T\text{-}IoU}=\frac{\sum_{f}|P_{f}\cap G_{f}|}{\sum_{f}|P_{f}\cup G_{f}|}.

    T-mIoU is the mean of T-IoU over the annotated objects of a clip, averaged over clips (0 to 1). An annotated object without a match scores 0, and predicted tracks without a match are not penalised. T-SR is the share of annotated objects whose per-view IoU exceeds 0.5 in every view in which they appear. The region similarity 𝒥\mathcal{J} (mean per-view IoU), the boundary measure ℱ\mathcal{F} (tolerance 0.8% of the image diagonal), and 𝒥&ℱ\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F} of DAVIS (Perazzi et al., 2016) are also reported. IGGT named T-mIoU and T-SR but defined them per view, averaging the IoU over views and counting an object as tracked when its prediction is non-empty in every view; the accumulated IoU, the IoU threshold of T-SR, and the greedy matching follow the evaluation of S4VY (Zhang et al., 2026c).

  • Prior work. IGGT reconstructs geometry and predicts 3D-consistent instance features with one transformer, trained with a 3D-consistent contrastive objective; IGGT4D (Zou et al., 2026) extends it to streaming 4D input; S4VY (Zhang et al., 2026c) adds persistent object queries to a feed-forward 4D geometry model. On the ten ScanNet clips under this metric, S4VY reports a T-mIoU of 0.803, against 0.781 for IGGT4D, 0.635 for SAM 2 (Ravi et al., 2024) with incremental object discovery, and 0.517 for IGGT.

Scene from Photo

  • Purpose. Whether the agent can build a single-image 3D scene reconstruction system: from one photograph of a furnished room, recover the camera, the room, and every piece of furniture as a complete object with plausible unseen sides, with physically based materials and lighting, so that a path tracer reproduces the photograph.

  • Source and construction. The photographs are those of HARMONY300 (Sun et al., 2026): 100 renders of 3D-FRONT rooms (Fu et al., 2021), which have ground-truth geometry, and 200 real photographs, half of moderate and half of high complexity. Each difficulty is split separately with a fixed seed (the renders stratified by their number of annotated objects) into 10, 10, and 20 photographs for development, validation, and test, giving 30, 30, and 60; the remaining 179 photographs are held out of every split, and one render whose image differs from its ground truth is excluded. On the renders the annotated furniture and its meshes come from the 3D-FRONT ground truth. On the real photographs up to eight pieces of furniture per photograph are annotated by Mask2Former (Cheng et al., 2022) panoptic segments of furniture classes (score at least 0.5, at least 0.5% of the image); on the renders this procedure recovers 85% of the annotated objects. The agent sees the development photographs with all labels.

  • Setting. The solution writes a Blender scene per photograph within 120 s per photograph; the evaluator renders it with Cycles from the scene’s own camera under fixed rules (only meshes, physically based shader nodes, non-emissive materials, at most 64 lights). It may use any public pretrained model on one GPU, but not HARMONY300, 3D-FRONT, 3D-FUTURE, or HARMONY’s code, and does not call the model being evaluated.

  • Starter solution. An empty room box in flat colors matched to the photograph, one ceiling light, and the same guessed camera with a 60° field of view for every photograph.

  • Metric. s=(A+O+G)/3s=(A+O+G)/3 in [0,1][0,1], with AA and OO averaged over all photographs and GG over the renders. Appearance A=13​[max⁡(0,1−NCLIP/0.25)+max⁡(0,1−PL/0.1)+1−LPIPS]A=\tfrac{1}{3}[\max(0,1-\mathrm{NCLIP}/0.25)+\max(0,1-\mathrm{PL}/0.1)+1-\mathrm{LPIPS}], where N-CLIP (one minus the cosine similarity of CLIP ViT-B/32 embeddings (Radford et al., 2021)) and the photometric loss PL are HARMONY’s metrics and LPIPS is that of Zhang et al. (2018). Objects O=meank​rk​min⁡(1,IoUk/0.5)O=\mathrm{mean}_{k}\,r_{k}\min(1,\mathrm{IoU}_{k}/0.5), where IoUk\mathrm{IoU}_{k} compares the meshes assigned to object kk with its mask and the realness rk=clip⁡((minj⁡Pj−0.5)/0.4,0,1)r_{k}=\mathrm{clip}((\min_{j}P_{j}-0.5)/0.4,0,1); PjP_{j} is the probability that Qwen3-VL-8B (Bai et al., 2025a), shown untextured views from four directions, judges the reconstruction a more real object than shortcut jj (its visible surface as a sheet, that sheet extruded to a prism, or its bounding box). Geometry G=(F0.1+F0.01+Fobj+Fhiddenobj)/400G=(F_{0.1}+F_{0.01}+F^{\mathrm{obj}}+F^{\mathrm{obj}}_{\mathrm{hidden}})/400, with HARMONY’s normalized scene F-scores in the protocol of Gen3DSR (Ardelean et al., 2025) (furniture only, both point sets normalized by their bounding box and aligned by ICP, thresholds 0.1 and 0.01) and per-object F-scores at 5 cm, in percent, after scaling by the median ratio of true to rendered depth; FhiddenobjF^{\mathrm{obj}}_{\mathrm{hidden}} counts recall only on the parts of the object the photograph does not show. A missing or unloadable scene, or one with more than 4 million triangles, renders black and has no geometry. For calibration, the true meshes textured with the photograph score 0.879 on the development renders, and HARMONY’s released reconstructions score 0.422 on the test split.

  • Prior work. HARMONY reconstructs such scenes by hierarchical agentic reasoning with a vision-language model and was compared with Gen3DSR, CAST (Yao et al., 2025), and SAM 3D (SAM 3D Team et al., 2025), among others.

Scene from Video

  • Purpose. Whether the agent can build a video-to-simulation pipeline: from the frames of an indoor video alone, estimate the cameras and reconstruct a scene of separate textured objects on a fixed background that has the true shape, reproduces the frames, and remains at rest under physical simulation.

  • Source and construction. The scenes are the nine released with HoloScene (Xia et al., 2025), each with frames, ground-truth cameras, per-object instance masks, a support graph, and a ground-truth surface. The test split is the six scenes evaluated by CoDimRecon (Xie et al., 2026): three Replica rooms (Straub et al., 2019) and three ScanNet++ captures (Yeshwanth et al., 2023). Validation is one iGibson house (Shen et al., 2021); development is another iGibson house and a game room filmed with a phone (undistorted). The iGibson and phone sequences keep every third frame. Each face of the ground-truth surface is labeled by the masks that see it, and each object is marked dynamic if it rests on the floor or on another object and static if it hangs from a wall or the ceiling. The agent sees the development frames with all labels and the scoring code.

  • Setting. The input is only the RGB frames, without cameras, masks, or depth, as in CoDimRecon. The solution writes a glTF scene (at most 4 million triangles) and a camera for every frame, within 1200 s per scene, on one GPU and 16 CPU cores. The scene is placed in the ground-truth frame by the similarity transform that aligns its cameras with the true ones, rendered unlit from the true cameras, and each mesh node is assigned to the object or background whose masks it covers most. Any public pretrained model may be used, but not the HoloScene release or its source datasets; the model being evaluated is not called.

  • Starter solution. An empty room box in the mean color of the frames, with every camera at one point.

  • Metric. Per scene, s=(G+A+P)/3s=(G+A+P)/3 with G=(F15​cm+NC)/200G=(\mathrm{F1}_{5\,\mathrm{cm}}+\mathrm{NC})/200 on 500,000 points of the whole scene, A=(SSIM+1−LPIPS)/2A=(\mathrm{SSIM}+1-\mathrm{LPIPS})/2 over all input frames (Wang et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2018), and PP the share of dynamic objects that are reconstructed (mask IoU at least 0.5) and stay in place; ss is averaged over scenes. Stability follows CoDimRecon: each dynamic object, decomposed into convex hulls by CoACD (Wei et al., 2022), is released alone in MuJoCo (Todorov et al., 2012) for 3 s with all else fixed, and falls if it tilts more than 30° or moves more than max⁡(5​cm,0.2​d)\max(5\,\mathrm{cm},0.2\,d), with dd its bounding-box diagonal. A missing or unloadable scene scores as empty. The ground-truth surface colored from the frames scores 0.936 on the test split.

  • Prior work. HoloScene reconstructs simulation-ready interactive scenes from a video given its cameras and instance masks. CoDimRecon reconstructs such scenes agentically from RGB views alone, representing objects as curves, surfaces, and volumes, and compares with HoloScene and an agent that writes the scene in Blender.

A.5  Perception

Visual Search

  • Purpose. Whether the agent can build a visual search procedure around a model with a limited field of view: questions concern small objects in photographs of 2K to 8K resolution, while each model call may contain at most one megapixel, so the solution must decide where to look.

  • Source and construction. The questions come from V*Bench (Wu and Xie, 2024) (191 multiple-choice questions on about 2K photographs: 115 on object attributes with four options, 76 on relative position with two) and HR-Bench 8K (Wang et al., 2025a) (200 questions with four options on 151 photographs of about 8K resolution, half on a single instance and half across instances; of its four rotated listings of each question one is drawn with a fixed seed). V*Bench is split by category and HR-Bench by photograph, so no photograph appears in two splits. The test split has 140 questions (70 from each benchmark). Development and validation are stratified subsets of 70 questions (33 and 37) and 80 questions (40 and 40). The agent sees the development photographs, questions, answers, and, for V*Bench, the boxes of the queried objects.

  • Setting. The solution answers each question with an option letter. It may call the model being evaluated on average at most five times per question, with at most 1024×10241024\times 1024 pixels per call in total; it may crop, resize, and run open-weight models on one GPU, and may not use either benchmark beyond the development split.

  • Starter solution. Shows the model the whole photograph reduced to one megapixel with the question, in a single call.

  • Metric. Accuracy over the questions of the split; a question without a valid letter counts as wrong. Accuracies on V*Bench and HR-Bench 8K are reported separately. Chance accuracy on the validation split is 0.303.

  • Prior work. V*Bench was introduced with SEAL, which guides a multimodal model to search the image for the queried region, and HR-Bench with a training-free method that divides the image into patches and combines their answers. Later methods explore zoomed regions as a tree (ZoomEye (Shen et al., 2025)) or learn to crop by reinforcement learning (DeepEyes (Zheng et al., 2026)).

Video Quality

  • Purpose. Whether the agent can turn a general multimodal model into a judge of perceptual video quality that agrees with people, both for real user videos and for generated videos.

  • Source and construction. The rated videos are 100 videos of YouTube-UGC (Wang et al., 2019), chosen from its 1,380 videos with mean opinion scores (MOS) excluding 4K: seven per content category for 14 categories (eight for sports and gaming), evenly spaced in MOS within each category. Each lasts 16.6 to 20 s at 360p to 1080p, and its MOS (1 to 5) averages 105 to 154 crowdsourced ratings from the subjective study of Yim et al. (2020). The pairs are 50 pairs from a public human-preference study of Veo 3.1 (Rapidata, 2025), each pitting Veo 3.1 against one of seven other text-to-video models on the same prompt (5 to 6 s clips). Each pair has 15 reliability-weighted crowd votes on three questions: prompt alignment, fewer visual artifacts, and overall preference, the last two judged without the prompt. A clip with more than 55% of the votes wins; otherwise the question is a tie. The videos are dealt in order of category and MOS, and the pairs in order of opposing model, into 30, 30, and 40 videos and 15, 15, and 20 pairs; the clip order in each pair is randomized. The agent sees the development videos, frames at two per second, and labels with vote shares and rating spreads.

  • Setting. The solution scores each video and answers the three questions for each pair. It may call the model being evaluated on average at most three times per item, with at most eight 1024×5761024\times 576 frames’ worth of pixels per call, and may run open-weight models on one GPU; it may not use the source datasets.

  • Starter solution. Asks for a rating from 1 to 5 given eight evenly spaced frames, and answers all three questions about a pair given six frames of each clip.

  • Metric. s=(SRCC+Acc)/2s=(\mathrm{SRCC}+\mathrm{Acc})/2, where SRCC is Spearman’s rank correlation (Spearman, 1904) between the solution’s scores and the MOS over the split’s videos (a video without a score receives the median of the others), and Acc is the share of non-tied pair questions answered correctly, pooled over the three criteria (a missing answer is wrong). PLCC and per-criterion accuracies are also reported. Chance is 0.25.

  • Prior work. YouTube-UGC was collected for video compression research, and its MOS serve to evaluate blind quality models such as VIDEVAL (Tu et al., 2021) and DOVER (Wu et al., 2023).

A.6  Infrastructure

VAE Decode

  • Purpose. Whether the agent can lower the latency of a fixed numerical computation, the video decoder of a generative model, without changing what it computes.

  • Source and construction. The computation is the decoder of the MiniMax H3 autoencoder (MiniMax, 2026b), a 36-layer vision transformer of about 2.4 billion parameters with FP32 weights run under FP16 autocast. It decodes a window of seven latent frames of 24 channels into 28 RGB frames, in 256×256256\times 256 tiles with at least 64 pixels of overlap and linear blending; the reference implementation and weights are pinned by hash. Inputs are latent windows of encoded videos at two sizes, 544×960544\times 960 and 480×832480\times 832 pixels, split by scene: 6 development, 6 validation, and 12 test scenes. Each request is either a real window with fresh noise (+0.05​𝒩​(0,1)+0.05\,\mathcal{N}(0,1)) or a synthetic stress window (Gaussian latents scaled per channel, clipped at ±5\pm 5). Per size and repetition there are four real and one stress request on development (two repetitions) and validation (six), and eight and two on test (six), so 20, 60, and 120 requests; no input repeats. The development windows are visible.

  • Setting. The solution is a decoder that receives latents in host memory and writes the full output into a host buffer. Custom Triton or CUDA kernels built from source, fusions, CUDA graphs, compilation, batching of tiles, and overlapping transfers are allowed. Lower precision, approximate or sparse attention, skipped tokens, tiles, or frames, reuse across requests, special treatment of stress windows, more than one GPU, shipped binaries, and existing optimized implementations of this decoder are not; accepted versions are reviewed for these rules. One H200, 90 s of setup, 30 s per request; the solution does not call the model being evaluated.

  • Starter solution. A direct eager PyTorch translation of the reference, bit-exact with it.

  • Metric. Every frame must be finite with a per-frame RMSE below 6.3×10−46.3\times 10^{-4} (1.9×10−31.9\times 10^{-3} for stress windows) and a maximum absolute error below 0.12 relative to the reference; these bounds are twice the largest error of legal reorderings, while FP16 accumulation, BF16, FP8, or dropped tokens exceed them. Fresh processes of the solution and of the starter serve the same requests side by side, timed from input to copied output. With cost C=t¯+tsetup/1024C=\bar{t}+t_{\mathrm{setup}}/1024 (t¯\bar{t} the mean latency), a repetition scores 0.75​log2​(Cstarter/C)544×960+0.25​log2​(Cstarter/C)480×8320.75\log_{2}(C_{\mathrm{starter}}/C)_{544\times 960}+0.25\log_{2}(C_{\mathrm{starter}}/C)_{480\times 832}; ss is the mean over repetitions without the highest and lowest. One gate failure, crash, or timeout, or a median cost or 95th-percentile latency above 1.5 times the starter’s, gives s=−1s=-1. The reported speedup is 2s2^{s}.

  • Prior work. The serving frameworks vLLM-Omni and SGLang (Zheng et al., 2024) include optimized implementations of the H3 decoder; these and code derived from them may not be used.

Appendix B Protocol and harness

This appendix specifies the parts of the protocol that Sections 3.2 and 3.3 describe only in outline: the structure of a round, the capabilities of the executor and the improver, the acceptance rule, the budget and the conditions under which a run ends, and the measures that keep the evaluation intact. The rules are identical for all models and tasks; the budget and two settings of the executor phase are fixed per task and listed in Table 10.

B.1  Round structure

A run begins by scoring the starter solution on the validation split, which gives the score against which the first candidate is compared. Each round then proceeds in five steps: an executor phase that produces a candidate solution; a check that reverts every change the executor made outside the files it may modify; the evaluation of the candidate on the validation split; the acceptance decision of Equation 2; and an improver phase that revises the harness.

The executor phase normally ends when the executor declares its work finished, and the solution in its final state becomes the candidate. It ends earlier when one of the executor’s evaluations on the development split exceeds the development score of the accepted solution by a fixed share of the distance between the starter’s validation score and the validation score of a strong known solution (Table 10); the solution as it was in that evaluation is then submitted. If the phase is interrupted before the executor finishes, because it reached its call limit, its time limit, or the budget, the best state that the executor’s development evaluations showed to exceed the accepted solution is submitted, and nothing is submitted if there is none. A round that leaves the solution unchanged does not use a validation evaluation.

B.2  Executor

The executor works in a copy of the run’s repository. Its tools allow it to run shell commands; to read, write, and edit files; to view images; to run experiments on the compute allocated to the task, including GPUs where the task provides them; to score the solution, or several variants of it at once, on the development split; and to query the remaining budget. It may write only to the solution, to a notes file that persists across rounds and is shared with the improver, and to a scratch directory that is emptied before each round. It observes development scores directly and the validation scores of earlier rounds through the run records, but it has no access to the validation or test data or to the evaluator. The starting harness allows 60 model calls per executor phase. Independently of the harness, the protocol stops a phase after the number of model calls given in Table 10 or after 180 minutes (600 minutes on the ARC tasks), and an experiment after 240 minutes.

B.3  Improver

After each round, the improver receives the executor’s transcript, its experiments and notes, and the scores of all rounds so far. It may modify the executor’s prompts, settings, control loop, and tools, as well as its own prompts, settings, acceptance rule, and a file of lessons that it maintains across rounds. A single improver phase may change at most 400 lines of the harness; a larger change is reverted in full. Every four rounds, the improver additionally reviews its own process: which kinds of harness changes were followed by accepted candidates and which by stalls, whether the acceptance rule is too strict or too permissive, and which lessons to record. Changes to the harness take effect from the following round. In the frozen-harness runs of Table 8, the improver is not run.

B.4  Acceptance rule

The margin δ\delta in Equation 2 is determined by the acceptance rule, which is part of the improver’s harness. In the starting harness, a candidate is accepted if its validation score exceeds that of the accepted solution by more than 2​σ2\sigma, where σ\sigma is the standard deviation of the starter’s validation score over repeated evaluations (Table 10). On tasks for which σ\sigma was not measured, it is set to zero, and any improvement on the validation split is accepted. Because the rule belongs to the harness, the improver may revise it. If the rule fails to return a decision, and in every run with a frozen harness, the starting rule δ=2​σ\delta=2\sigma is applied.

B.5  Budget and termination

A run ends at the first of the following events: the wall-clock time, GPU hours, tokens (input, including cached input, and output), or cost in dollars reach the task’s limit; the number of validation evaluations reaches its limit; the round cap is reached; or five consecutive rounds produce neither a candidate nor a change to the harness, a rule that is not applied on LIBERO-MAX and LIBERO-PRO. The budget is checked before each model call, experiment, and development evaluation and is charged when each of them ends, so that calls running concurrently can exceed a limit by at most their combined cost. A submitted candidate is evaluated on the validation split even when the budget is exhausted. Model calls that the evaluator makes on the validation and test splits, for tasks whose solution calls the model, are recorded but not charged. Periods during which the model provider is unavailable are not charged either, and a phase interrupted by such an outage is repeated. After the run, the final solution and every accepted solution are scored on the test split (Section 3.3).

Table 10 gives the limits of each task. On a given task, all models have the same limits, with the following exceptions. Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemini 4 Argon are stopped after 80 model calls per executor phase on Active Search, Ego-Exo Memory, 3D Tracking, Visual Search, and Video Quality. On Active Search, the dollar limit for open-weight models is 250. On RoboLab, the runs of Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, and GPT-6.1 Sol have 240 GPU hours. On Image Editing, the runs of Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, and both Gemini models have 60 wall-clock hours and a dollar limit of 150. On Kinematics and Mass, the wall-clock limit of every model other than Claude Opus 5.5 is the time used by the run of Claude Opus 5.5 (11.3 and 11.0 hours). On Embodied-SWE and Spatial-VSI, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is limited to the tokens used by the run of Claude Opus 5.5 (22M and 21M). On 3D Tracking, Claude Sonnet 5.5 has a dollar limit of 50. On RoboCasa, Muse Spark 1.3 has 48 GPU hours and 80M tokens. On RoboDojo and RoboCasa, runs that continued past round 10 are scored with the solution they had after round 10.

B.6  Isolation and integrity

After every phase, any change outside the paths that the phase may modify, including changes made through shell commands, is reverted and recorded as a violation; the evaluator, the data splits, and the protocol therefore cannot be altered by the agent. Files larger than 5 MB are excluded from the run’s repository. If a phase crashes in two consecutive rounds, the harness is restored to the last version that completed a round without a crash. When a phase ends, all processes it started are terminated, so that no process left running can modify the solution afterwards. All model calls, experiments, and development evaluations are routed through the benchmark, which charges them to the budget and records them.
